items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) have developed a dexterous robotic hand designed to make advanced manipulation more accessible. The PHD Hand combines 3D-printed components with relatively simple mechanical systems. Its design aims to reduce manufacturing costs and maintenance without sacrificing functionality. Associate Professor Cong Wang and doctoral student Neel Adwani developed the hand. Their research paper will appear at the IEEE Humanoids conference in December 2026. It examines the hand’s mechanical design, movement capabilities, and AI-assisted control. Hospital inspiration Wang’s path toward the design began during a hospital stay in 2024. He spent that period without access to phones, computers, or other camera-equipped devices. A notebook and pen became his primary tools for developing ideas. His experience also changed how he viewed robotic manipulation. Watching medical professionals perform routine tasks made him consider the limitations of existing robotic hands. “Every small task can be a huge challenge for the robot hands today,” Wang said. He had already explored robotic manipulation through an earlier chopsticks project. Wang also saw an opportunity to rethink the engineering behind commercial dexterous hands. He considered many existing models too expensive, fragile, and difficult to maintain. His goal became creating a simpler equivalent of the Ford Model T. After returning to campus, Wang shared his concept with Adwani. Adwani subsequently led the development team. Research assistant Muhaiminul Akash, undergraduate Saffia Ouali, and high school student Ethan Liu also contributed. Simple mechanics, greater accessibility Most industrial robotic hands rely on tendon-driven mechanisms. These systems offer considerable dexterity but often require expensive components and regular maintenance. Linkage-driven alternatives simplify the mechanics but frequently limit independent finger movements. The PHD Hand, short for printable humanoid dexterous, takes another approach. Its design reduces the number of miniature moving components. That makes fabrication possible with an affordable desktop 3D printer. The hand uses printed joints and knuckles with narrow internal channels. Metal rods run through these openings to support finger movement. Springs sit inside the fingertips, while readily available hobby servos provide actuation. Another useful feature concerns what happens when electrical power disappears. The fingers can return to a preset neutral position without continued power. That behavior could prove valuable in applications where unexpected shutdowns create problems. Users control the hand through browser-based software. Its interface allows them to drag movements into position with a mouse. The system can also accommodate typed or spoken instructions through large language model integration. Teaching robots everyday manipulation Adwani wants to push the hand beyond basic gripping demonstrations. His doctoral research will explore how robots manipulate everyday objects in more natural ways. Consider picking up a spatula from its handle’s opposite end. A person can quickly adjust their grip and reorient the utensil. Programming a robot to perform that sequence presents a considerably harder problem. The team also plans to investigate tactile sensing. Cameras could eventually help the hand recognize objects and coordinate more complex movements. Researchers hope to demonstrate tasks such as opening eyeglasses cases and tightening jar lids. Those experiments will likely expose new engineering challenges. Adwani acknowledged that the team cannot anticipate every difficulty before testing begins. Wang also took a personal lesson from the project. His hospital stay made him reconsider the importance of looking after himself. Unexpectedly, stepping away from digital distractions also gave him more room to think.

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at Stanford University have demonstrated an unusual electrical conductor that becomes more efficient as its wires get narrower, potentially overcoming a major limitation of copper wiring in next-generation computer chips. The team tested nanoribbons made from niobium phosphide (NbP), a topological semimetal that conducts electricity differently from conventional metals. The researchers found that its electrical resistivity decreases as the ribbons become narrower, allowing the material to outperform similarly sized copper conductors at extremely small dimensions. The study could offer a new approach to building the nanoscale interconnects that connect billions of transistors and other components inside modern processors. Copper has long served as the primary wiring material in computer chips. However, as manufacturers shrink these connections to just a few nanometers, electrons increasingly scatter from wire surfaces and grain boundaries. This raises electrical resistance, wastes energy as heat and makes signal transmission less efficient. The problem becomes particularly important in high-density chips, where billions of connections must operate within a small area. Semimetal reverses copper limits To investigate an alternative, the researchers fabricated flat niobium phosphide nanoribbons as narrow as 5 to 6 nanometers and approximately 1.5 nanometers thick. At a cross-sectional area of about 9 square nanometers, the nanoribbons achieved an electrical resistivity of 18 ± 4.1 micro-ohm centimetres at room temperature. The researchers reported that this was lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable dimensions. Unlike copper, where most electrical current travels through the material’s core, niobium phosphide can carry a greater proportion of current along its surfaces and edges. This behaviour is linked to its topological properties, particularly spin-momentum locking, which reduces electron backscattering. As the nanoribbons become narrower, surface and edge conduction contribute more significantly to the overall current. The team also found that this conduction remained relatively insensitive to manufacturing imperfections, including surface roughness and oxidation. Eric Pop, a professor of electrical engineering at Stanford and senior author of the study, compared the problem with water flowing through pipes. A wide pipe carries water efficiently, but narrowing it to the size of a straw makes its walls increasingly restrictive. Similarly, surface scattering makes copper less efficient as its dimensions shrink. Niobium phosphide, by contrast, allows electrons to travel more efficiently along its surfaces at these extremely small scales. Chip manufacturing potential The researchers said the material’s performance at room temperature and compatibility with industry-standard fabrication techniques make it promising for future semiconductor manufacturing. The team used top-down nanofabrication methods to pattern the material into narrow ribbons, rather than relying on a specialized manufacturing approach designed exclusively for laboratory demonstrations. However, the material is not yet ready to replace copper in commercial processors. Researchers still need to investigate its long-term endurance, fabrication compatibility, and behavior across different operating temperatures. The team is also examining other semimetals that could offer similar or better electrical performance. The work involved researchers from Stanford University, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Pennsylvania State University, the Weizmann Institute of Science and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The findings suggest that topological semimetals could provide an alternative route to reducing resistance in increasingly compact chip interconnects, where conventional copper wiring faces growing physical limitations. The study was published in the journal Nature .

items.descriptionOriginal: Σήμερα Πέμπτη, 26 Νοεμβρίου , σύμφωνα με το εορτολόγιο τιμάται η μνήμη των Στυλιανού Παφλαγώνος, Νίκωνος προστάτη Λακωνίας . Τα ονόματα που γιορτάζουν σήμερα είναι τα εξής: Στυλιανός, Στέργιος, Στέλιος, Στελής, Τέλης, Τέλιος, Στέλα, Στεργιανή, Στεργιούλα, Στυλιανή, Στέλλα, Τέλα, Τελία, Τελίτσα, Στελίνα, Νίκων. Όσιος Στυλιανός ο Παφλαγόνας Ο Όσιος Στυλιανός ήταν γιος πλουσίων γονέων (που μάλλον γεννήθηκε στην Παφλαγονία, χωρίς αυτό να είναι σίγουρο, διότι εκεί φυλασσόταν και ιερό λείψανο του), διδάχτηκε νωρίς απ’ αυτούς να είναι εγκρατής και να θεωρεί το χρήμα μέσο για την ανακούφιση και περίθαλψη των φτωχών και των αρρώστων. Αφού έτσι ανατράφηκε, και οι γονείς του πέθαναν, διαμοίρασε όλη την κληρονομιά του και πήγε σαν ασκητής στην έρημο. Εκεί γνωρίστηκε με άλλους ασκητές, που ζούσε μαζί τους με αδελφική αγάπη, χριστιανική συγκατάβαση και επιείκεια. Δεν λύπησε ποτέ κανένα, μεγάλη του χαρά μάλιστα, ήταν να επαναφέρει τη γαλήνη στις ταραγμένες ψυχές. Η φήμη της θαυμαστής ασκητικής του ζωής έφθασε μέχρι τις πόλεις, και πολλοί έτρεχαν να τον βρουν για να ζητήσουν απ’ αυτόν τις πνευματικές του οδηγίες. Ο όσιος Στυλιανός, παρά την ερημική ζωή του, έτρεφε στοργή και συμπάθεια προς τα παιδιά, που τόσο αγαπούσε και ο Κύριος . Αν, έλεγε, η ταπεινοφροσύνη αποτελεί θεμέλιο των αρετών, η παιδική ηλικία από τη φύση της είναι περισσότερο ενάρετη, απ’ ότι οι μεγαλύτεροι των φιλοσόφων. Πολλές φορές οι γονείς έφερναν προς αυτόν τα παιδιά τους, και τότε η αγαλλίαση του οσίου ήταν πολύ μεγάλη. Ο Θεός βραβεύοντας το Ιερό αυτό αίσθημα του, προίκισε τον όσιο με το χάρισμα να θεραπεύει τα άρρωστα παιδιά και να καθιστά εύτεκνους άτεκνες γυναίκες . Ο Όσιος Στυλιανός κοιμήθηκε πλήρης ήμερων αλλά και αρετών . Ανατολή ήλιου: 07:17 – Δύση ήλιου: 17:07 Σελήνη 16.8 ημερών www.ertnews.gr

items.title: Από το πλύσιμο των πιάτων στο τραγούδι για εκατομμύρια: Ο Talwiinder λέει ειλικρινής για το πώς δίδαξε τον εαυτό του μουσική
items.titleOriginal: From Washing Dishes to Singing for Millions: Talwiinder Gets Candid About How He Taught Himself Music
items.description: Τι κάνεις όταν θέλεις να γίνεις μουσικός, αλλά το δοκιμαστήριο σου είναι ένα φαστ φουντ και ο χρόνος εξάσκησής σου ξεκινά αφού φύγει ο τελευταίος πελάτης; Για περισσότερα από τέσσερα χρόνια, η απάντηση του Talwiinder ήταν να τραγουδάει πλένοντας πιάτα και κλείνοντας το Subway. Άρχισε να εργάζεται εκεί στην Τάξη 10, προσαρμόζοντας το riyaaz (μουσική πρακτική) γύρω από την παραγγελία του πελάτη…
items.descriptionOriginal: What do you do when you want to become a musician, but your rehearsal room is a fast-food outlet and your practice time begins after the last customer has left? For more than four years, Talwiinder's answer was to sing while washing dishes and closing Subway. He started working there in Class 10, fitting riyaaz (music practice) around customer orders and closing duties. Without formal music training, he used the time after serving customers to practise his singing. Today, his music has travelled far beyond that counter. 'Pal Pal', made with Afusic and Ali Soomro, caught the attention of British DJ and producer Fred again.., who played the track during a livestream. Talwiinder saw it just like everyone else watching. It was, he says, "a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene". Between those closing shifts and the livestream were years of teaching himself music, writing songs and continuing to create despite rejection from music labels. From serving customers to writing songs Talwiinder has been singing since he was three or four, but he says the decision to build a life around music came when he began writing songs of his own. Singing was something he loved; songwriting gave that love somewhere to go . The 'Pal Pal' livestream moment connected a Punjabi collaboration with audiences beyond its listening community. Photograph: ( Instagram/@talwiinder ) "The moment I started to write my own songs, I knew I had to release these tracks for people who need it more than me," he tells The Better India . "Once I got into songwriting, I knew this is what I want to do for the rest of my life." There was no ready-made route into the industry. He spent more than four years at Subway, starting in Class 10, and remembers the job fondly for what it taught him about people. "It taught me communication, reading people's energy and having one-on-one conversations with customers to the point where I knew their whole order the moment they stepped in the store," he says. He learnt to run the store by himself. When the rush was over, he had time alone with his thoughts. "That alone time was often used to do riyaaz while cleaning dishes and closing the store," he says. "I loved every bit of that job and never felt like I wanted to quit." His music moves between Punjabi and international listening spaces, opening possibilities for cross-cultural collaboration. Interestingly, someone who once spent hours interacting with customers now prefers to keep conversations brief. He says he prefers texting to phone calls and often avoids conversations because talking for too long tires his throat and voice. He likes to "talk with eyes" and use very few words. He even has a WhatsApp display picture that reads, "Don't call me, text me." Through the songs he writes, however, Talwiinder communicates with millions of listeners. Learning how to express himself through music has involved years of listening to and understanding his own voice. How he taught himself music Without formal music training, Talwiinder learnt by making songs and returning to them. He advises beginners with a laptop or computer to invest in a home-recording setup, which he estimates can cost around $150 to $200, rather than waiting for a professional studio or teacher. "Record yourself as much as you can," he says. "You will understand your voice better. When the time comes and you're in a proper studio with top-notch equipment, you won't be so lost, but excited to go full beast mode." For listeners discovering Punjabi music abroad, Talwiinder offers an entry point into Punjabi sounds. Listening to these recordings helps a singer recognise what needs work and gradually develop a sound of their own. It is something aspiring musicians can begin doing with basic equipment at home. Over time, Talwiinder has also learnt when to stop working on a song and let listeners hear it. He does not believe there is a magical point at which a track becomes perfect. "The song is never ready; there will always be something that can be added or taken out," he says. "You have to trust your gut and give your 100% in stitching the song together, and once it's out, make peace with it and move on to the next song." With every release comes a public tally of streams, views and likes, but Talwiinder says he has never made numbers the measure of his work. He recalls gaining more than four million Instagram followers in a month without paid promotions. He says he has never bought fake views or likes, or followed trends. His focus, he says, is on doing justice to the music, while listeners decide whether to return to it. When he does not feel like starting something new, he returns to his unfinished tracks. "I have way too many unfinished songs," he says. He chooses his favourites and starts finishing them, turning a creative block into a chance to reopen old work. When music labels turned him down The years were not without rejection. Talwiinder remembers approaching labels that did not want to associate with his music. Among the tracks he mentions is 'Khayaal'. The singer's visual aesthetic draws from alternative music culture rather than conventional Punjabi entertainment imagery. "They told me indirectly and did not want to associate with my music," he says. "Funny thing is I still see those labels coming back and asking to work together." He kept making music, including songs that did not immediately find their moment. 'Haseen' was written and recorded in 2019 but released six years later. He says he would not change his older music simply because he has grown as an artist. "I believe good music does not have an expiration date," he says. A song does not lose its value, in his view, because it has been waiting in a folder. With 'Pal Pal', Talwiinder experienced what it was like for his music to reach someone he had not expected. The collaboration with Afusic and Ali Soomro caught the attention of Fred again.. When the British DJ played the track during a livestream, Talwiinder did not hear about it through a label or a carefully arranged announcement. He saw it on the stream, like everybody else. "It caught me by surprise," he says. "It was a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene." With his signature face paint and unconventional styling, Talwiinder has carved out a recognisable space in contemporary music. Having experienced rejection himself, Talwiinder now wants to help other aspiring musicians find people they can work with. Asked what he would do if a young artist arrived with little money and no industry connections, Talwiinder says he would first listen. If the work felt genuine and original, he would connect the artist with his community and suggest collaborators, giving them somewhere to belong. For someone who spent years practising after work and learning to make music on his own, being able to offer another young artist a place to begin is something he now looks forward to.

Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

items.descriptionOriginal: XPENG has unveiled a new physical-intelligence architecture and its IRON humanoid robot, outlining plans to bring the machine into its retail stores in 2027 as the Chinese automaker expands into robotics and autonomous mobility. The company introduced its Turing Physical AI Architecture, also called VLA 3.0, at its eighth AI Day in Guangzhou on November 25. The framework connects AI models with computing, perception, control systems, and physical hardware across intelligent vehicles and humanoid robots. XPENG said the architecture has three systems operating at different speeds. System 0 coordinates hardware functions, including power, energy, communication, and execution, while feeding information about the body’s state back into the AI loop. System 1, powered by the company’s VLA 2.0 model, interprets the surrounding environment and translates it into real-time actions. System 2 handles higher-level cognition, using vision-language task planning and an agent runtime system to interpret objectives and coordinate complex tasks. The company said the three layers create a feedback loop in which physical actions inform subsequent decisions. Its latest VLA 2.0 model, version 6.4.0, supports agent-driven closed-loop training, which XPENG said increases training speed by 10 to 12 times. IRON targets retail roles IRON, which made its first public appearance at the event, has 76 degrees of freedom and more than 1,500 tactile sensing points. XPENG said sensors cover more than 80 percent of key body areas, while three proprietary Turing AI chips support onboard models and whole-body control. The robot combines multimodal understanding and task planning with navigation, manipulation, and safety monitoring. It can navigate autonomously, receive tasks through voice or app instructions, charge itself, and report abnormal conditions, according to the company. XPENG plans to begin training IRON as a store assistant in its retail outlets in the first quarter of 2027. Its official public release is targeted for the second quarter. The company has established a robot data factory covering more than 250 scenarios and 15 job categories. Its automated assembly line includes more than 600 holographic quality-inspection items and over 1,000 tests for complete robots and key components. Vehicles join robotics push XPENG is extending its physical-intelligence strategy into vehicles. Its X-VMC 2.0 motion-control system connects propulsion, braking, steering and suspension, allowing software to coordinate driving, safety, comfort and energy management. A feature called VLA Adaptive Deceleration adjusts braking and energy recovery when a driver releases the accelerator. XPENG said tests in urban congestion showed a 12.4 percent increase in usable driving range compared with having energy recovery switched off. The feature is scheduled for its first over-the-air rollout in December 2026. The company said its robotaxi program moved from staffed to driverless road testing in eight months and obtained an L4 demonstration-operation qualification in Guangzhou. Driverless passenger tests have begun, with demonstration operations in selected areas planned by the end of 2026. XPENG’s first purpose-built robotaxi, the YOYO-01, is scheduled for release in 2027. Its ARIDGE business is advancing a manned electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft program towards airworthiness certification. XPENG aims to use a shared technology foundation across vehicles, robots, and flying vehicles, while adapting systems for different hardware and tasks.

items.descriptionOriginal: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Mark Schroeder , καθηγητή φιλοσοφίας στο USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons . Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Υπάρχουν λίγα μεγαλύτερα συναισθήματα t…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Mark Schroeder , a professor of philosophy at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts, and Sciences, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . There are few greater feelings than the sense of heartfelt gratitude to another human being who has done you a solid. Sincere thanks and reciprocation are part of the glue that binds us in human relationships. But sometimes you’re just not feeling it. You know that you have benefited from what someone has done for you, but you don’t really feel grateful to them for doing it. Most teenagers go through this period with their parents. Maybe you take your partner or colleague for granted. For me, 14 years ago, it was my mother-in-law. She had upended her life to move from South Dakota to California to live with my wife and me to assist with childcare after our daughter was born; no other source of childcare fit with our demanding work schedules and my commute. She made a huge sacrifice that transformed our lives, but there were moments when I really struggled to feel grateful. Since that time, I’ve come to devote much of my research as a philosopher to studying how the way that we interpret each other as people shapes our relationships . That work has helped me to understand why I struggled to be grateful — and taught me a little bit about how to do better. Personal Gratitude I’ve found that the hardest part of feeling grateful to someone is the “to” part. It is one thing to be impersonally grateful that something happened and another thing to be personally grateful to someone for doing it. These are not the same. Both forms of gratitude require seeing something as a benefit. And they both require a humble recognition of how easily things could have been otherwise. When the rain ends a drought, an atheist can feel grateful that the tomatoes will survive. But the atheist isn’t grateful “to” anyone for the rain. AP Photo/Mahesh Kumar A Priests offer prayers to Varuna, the Hindu god of rain, as they stand in the Osman Sagar on the outskirts of Hyderabad, India, on July 16, 2013. Personal gratitude requires more than impersonal gratitude. It is an example of what the philosopher Peter Strawson calls a “participant” attitude : an attitude that we have toward people, but not toward things. And a large theme in my work is that participant attitudes such as gratitude involve giving someone credit for what the attitude responds to. But which benefits we give people credit for is complicated. As philosophers such as Tony Manela have argued, actions motivated primarily by money, self-interest, or insecurity don’t merit personal gratitude , even when they benefit you. Actions motivated by love, generosity, or concern, on the other hand — or other “pro-social” motives — do. Sometimes people fail to feel gratitude because they take someone for granted, not noticing how easily they could have done otherwise. This wasn’t my problem with my mother-in-law. It was obvious that she didn’t have to move across the country to live with us. But it was hard to avoid noticing that she had always wanted to live in California. Sometimes it is hard to feel grateful because of how we interpret someone’s motives. They could have done otherwise, but we don’t think their action was really “about us.” Bad Motives Are Easy to Find Sometimes ungenerous motives can help people to be generous. Your child’s kindergarten teacher isn’t a volunteer. They may be a naturally generous person — but still, they probably wouldn’t be working with your child on spelling, arithmetic, and handling adversity if they weren’t getting a paycheck. It’s still appropriate to be grateful to them. Their financial incentive to show up for work enables their generosity, rather than competing with it. svetikd—E+/Getty Images Your child’s teacher might be generous, but their job enables them to act on that generosity every day. Elementary school teachers are not alone. After all, people’s decisions are often driven by many factors: some that merit gratitude and others that don’t. So if you go looking for selfish motives, you are bound to find some . Take your partner, for example. They do something that benefits you: buying you flowers, filling your tank with gas, or finally taking their turn to wash the dishes. They are partly motivated by generosity, love, or communal spirit. But, as in any close relationship, sometimes they may be hoping to get something out of it : reciprocation, maybe, or getting you off their back. It matters which of these you interpret as their “true” motive: Seeing it one way opens you up to gratitude, while the other precludes it. What Are “True” Motives? The distinction between someone’s “true” motive and the other motives that enable it looks like the distinction between causes and enabling conditions . For example, when you drop a wine glass, the fragility of the glass enables the drop to cause the break, but it isn’t itself a cause of the break — the drop is. In the case of the falling glass, there’s a clear, objective answer to what caused the break and what merely enabled it. But I believe that relating to people is deeply different than understanding physical things. The key question in whether to be grateful to someone isn’t about which motives count as “causes.” It is about which cause we need to bring into focus in order to see the other person more clearly for who they are . See It Their Way In other words, it’s at least partly a matter of perspective. If someone does you a favor, but you know they’re hoping for something in return, you can see that as their “true” motive. But you don’t have to see it that way. Instead, you could see that motive as the condition they need for their generosity to thrive. Shifting perspectives isn’t easy. When you’re doubting someone’s motives , their lack of generosity can feel obvious. But it helps to remember that people tend to believe they’re acting generously . If you want to respond with gratitude, try seeing them as they see themselves. What if that doesn’t work? Well, the next best thing to being grateful to someone is being grateful for them. Starting there is a good way to remind yourself of why you value this relationship in the first place. And it can be enough to simply say “thanks” and mean it. items.descriptionOriginal: Neuralink has received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal clinical trial in the country for an implantable brain-computer interface (BCI). The study will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the company’s technology in people with severe paralysis caused by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Announcing the development on November 25, Neuralink said the trial builds on its ongoing early feasibility studies in the US, Canada and the UK, which have involved more than 30 implanted participants. Together, these participants have contributed thousands of hours of real-world use of the company’s brain-computer interface. The LINK Pivotal Study will examine how effectively participants can use the Neuralink system to control digital devices through thought. The company said the research would focus on functional outcomes that could improve independence in everyday life, alongside the long-term safety and reliability of the implant. Neuralink said enrolment for the study is now open, with the programme expected to expand across multiple clinical sites in the US. Implant reads brain signals The system being evaluated uses Neuralink’s N1 Implant, which records neural activity through fine electrode threads placed in the brain’s motor cortex, the region associated with movement. The implant detects electrical signals associated with intended movements and translates them into commands that allow users to interact with digital devices. Participants can learn to move a computer cursor by imagining moving their hand, without physically moving their limbs. Neuralink’s existing Telepathy programme has demonstrated cursor navigation and mouse functions, including left, right and middle clicks. Participants have also used the technology for activities such as messaging, browsing the internet, writing code, creating digital artwork and playing video games. The implant is inserted using the company’s R1 surgical robot, which places the fine electrode threads into the brain. The N1 device sits within the skull, with no external wires or battery pack. It communicates wirelessly with a computer and can also be charged wirelessly through the scalp. Neuralink’s clinical-trial information says participants undergo surgery under general anaesthesia. The company’s published study pathway includes health screening, brain imaging, implantation, device training and follow-up assessments. Pivotal trial marks milestone The new study represents a move beyond Neuralink’s earlier-stage human testing. Its PRIME programme was designed as an early feasibility study to evaluate the initial safety and functionality of the N1 Implant, R1 Robot and associated software in people with paralysis. A pivotal trial is a later-stage clinical investigation intended to generate evidence about a medical device’s safety and effectiveness for a specific intended use. Such evidence can support a subsequent regulatory application, although successful completion does not guarantee marketing authorisation. Importantly, the FDA’s approval to launch LINK does not mean the Neuralink implant has been approved for general medical use. The company continues to describe its devices as investigational and available only through authorised clinical research. Neuralink’s trial information identifies adults living with ALS as eligible for the pivotal study. Its published participation pathway also outlines follow-up assessments extending to 24 months after implantation, allowing researchers to monitor device performance and participant safety over time. The company’s announcement did not disclose the planned number of participants or provide a detailed breakdown of clinical sites. The milestone could bring Neuralink closer to establishing the clinical evidence needed for a future regulatory submission. However, the pivotal study will need to demonstrate that the implant can provide reliable digital-device control while maintaining an acceptable safety profile over an extended period.

items.descriptionOriginal: A new solar-powered electric vehicle charging system was unveiled at the ongoing Genera trade show, which began Tuesday, November 24, in Madrid, Spain. ​The facility, named Urven Charger Park, was developed jointly by two Spanish energy companies, Urven and Bexie Energy. The former builds photovoltaic canopies for carports, while the latter integrates the electric vehicle charging infrastructure into these covered parking areas. ​According to company officials, the EV chargers are integrated directly into the supporting pillars of solar carports connected in series, eliminating the need for separate charging stations. Self-supporting structures ​Urven’s solar -powered system is designed to stand on prefabricated concrete bases, eliminating the need for excavation or poured concrete foundations. ​This distinguishes it from conventional solar carports. The bases can simply be placed on the ground before the steel structure is bolted into place. ​”It is essentially a plug-and-play solution,” said Iñaki Llana, director of Urven. “Everything leaves our factory fully prepared so that assembling the structure is like putting together Lego pieces,” she added. ​In addition to simplifying installation, the prefabricated concrete bases showcased at the event provide the weight needed to stabilize the photovoltaic carports. Weighing approximately 5,500 pounds (2,500 kg) and 7,700 pounds (3,500 kg), the bases keep the self-supporting structures securely in place, helping prevent them from tipping, shifting, or lifting in strong winds. Comes in four different models ​According to company officials, the system is available in four configurations: two single-carport and two double-carport models, all with app-based controls. ​The single-carport model is equipped with two 22-kW AC charging points with Type 2 charging cables, while the double-carport version features a 60-kW DC fast charger that can be activated using a radio-frequency identification (RFID) card in addition to app-based controls. ​Both the single- and double-carport configurations also include smart features such as an LCD display, LED status indicators, and Wi-Fi, Ethernet, Bluetooth, and 4G connectivity. ​The models showcased at the trade fair used bifacial solar modules measuring 1,134 mm × 2,384 mm. However, the company said the structures can be adapted to accommodate different panel formats. ​Beyond the solar panels, the carports can also house battery energy storage systems , inverters, electrical protection equipment, static or dynamic advertising displays, and white or RGB LED lighting, according to Llana. All components can be customized to meet customer requirements, she added. ​The solar-powered carports are designed for residential, commercial, industrial, and healthcare applications, ranging from compact two-vehicle residential installations to larger structures that can accommodate vans and motorhomes. ​However, the company said it still conducts a preliminary structural analysis for each project based on its location and site-specific requirements. While the current designs remain more expensive than conventional solar carports, officials said the prefabricated system helps keep overall project costs under control. ​”We achieve significant cost reductions at the overall project level by reducing installation times, disruption to parking operations and, above all, labor requirements,” Llana said . ​

Το δίκτυο θα μετακινούσε σημαντικό υπολογιστικό φόρτο εργασίας πέρα ​​από αυτό της Γης…
items.descriptionOriginal: SpaceX has received federal approval to pursue one of the largest satellite infrastructure projects ever proposed. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized Elon Musk’s company to deploy up to 1 million satellites under its Starmind orbital computing initiative. The network would move substantial computing workloads beyond Earth’s atmosphere as demand for advanced computing infrastructure continues to grow. The authorization marks the first time the FCC has approved an entire constellation dedicated to space-based data centers. SpaceX wants to distribute computing hardware across orbit and use the resulting processing capacity to support applications on Earth. How Starmind will process data Starmind would operate as an interconnected network of orbital computing modules. Each satellite would process information in space before transmitting results back to Earth. The architecture would shift some computing workloads away from conventional terrestrial data centers. SpaceX plans to connect the satellites through optical inter-satellite links. These laser-based connections would allow spacecraft to exchange information without depending entirely on ground stations. Radiofrequency communications would provide additional connectivity when necessary. The FCC has also authorized backup radio links for telemetry, tracking, and command operations. These connections would help SpaceX monitor its satellites and maintain control during emergencies. The approval covers the 18.8–19.3 GHz downlink and 28.6–29.1 GHz uplink frequency bands. Moving computing infrastructure into orbit could address several limitations facing terrestrial data centers. Large facilities require substantial electricity and sophisticated cooling infrastructure to handle demanding computing workloads. SpaceX argues that orbital facilities could harness solar energy more efficiently while reducing some of these requirements. However, operating powerful computers in space introduces significant engineering challenges. Electronic hardware generates considerable heat during intensive processing. Satellites must dissipate that heat without conventional air-based cooling systems. SpaceX must also demonstrate that it can manufacture, launch, and maintain such an enormous satellite network. The company’s developing Starship rocket could play an important role in making deployment economically viable. Massive deployment challenge The FCC’s authorization does not mean SpaceX can immediately deploy its entire proposed constellation. The company must meet several deployment milestones over the coming years. SpaceX must place its first operational satellite in orbit by November 2033. The authorization requires 100,000 operational satellites by November 2035. The company must reach half its approved constellation by November 2038. Full deployment must follow by November 2040. Even with regulatory approval, achieving those targets will require substantial advances in launch capacity and satellite manufacturing. The FCC also left certain aspects of SpaceX’s proposal unresolved. The company must address additional regulatory requirements concerning satellite disposal. The agency will continue reviewing other orbital data center proposals through its established procedures. SpaceX also announced Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued Class A common share to every active Trump Account. These tax-advantaged investment accounts help American children build long-term savings. SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary. We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans. Today, we are committing one SpaceX share to millions of American children… — SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 25, 2026 Musk will personally match the number of shares contributed by SpaceX. The commitment fulfills a pledge he made on X in October 2026 to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States. At the time, the proposed contribution covered approximately 73 million children and carried an estimated value of $10.7 billion. SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell separately announced a personal contribution exceeding 2 million company shares. The commitments extend the company’s ownership initiative to younger Americans as it pursues its ambitious plans across space transportation and orbital computing.

items.descriptionOriginal: Family, friends, football – Turkey Day is many things, but food is always at the center. Making the best side dish for Thanksgiving can occasionally feel like playing against the clock. Do you know how to make it exactly like grandma did? How are you supposed to keep it at optimum serving temperature when the turkey still has an hour to go? And most importantly, will the final product get the approval of that one aunt who never seems to like anything? No playbook, however, has been as fiercely guarded as NFL coach Andy Reid’s secret recipe for mac-and-cheese . For years, football fans whispered about the Kansas City Chiefs coach’s legendary cheesy creation. Whenever reporters asked for details, he stayed notoriously tight-lipped. Could anyone make him give up his culinary game plan ? Players, coaches, even The Washington Post tried to crack the case . Now, journalist Pablo Torre has finally uncovered the full recipe. The tasty mystery behind the mac-and-cheese This cheesy journey began at an airport terminal in 2018. Writer Charles McDonald bumped into Reid , and the conversation turned to Thanksgiving food. McDonald says that Reid pulled up various recipes on his phone. Then the famous coach offhandedly mentioned that his creamy version of the pasta classic features seven different cheeses. In the video, he only lists six cheeses: fontina, mozzarella, parmesan, sharp cheddar, gouda, and gruyere. The mystery of the seventh cheese left fans obsessed with tracking down the final ingredient. Why football fans craved Coach Reid’s recipe Andy Reid is famous for much more than his trademark moustache. He’s known for drawing up clever offensive plays that lead to big wins on the field. His warm nature and love of comfort food made the mystery of the missing cheese all the more irresistible. Whenever Reid was pressed for more details, he kept fans guessing. He famously joked that he could not give away the secrets because he might open a restaurant. For eight long years, fans debated what the missing seventh cheese could be. That lingering curiosity turned a simple side dish into one of sports media’s favorite running jokes. The seventh cheese and the surprise ingredient Journalist and podcaster Pablo Torre decided it was time to crack the case once and for all. He teamed up with Charles McDonald , former Chiefs tackle Mitchell Schwartz , and celebrity chef David Chang . The investigation revealed the missing ingredient. It turned out to be something no one had considered before: Velveeta. According to Reid, a little bit of the processed cheese product helps keep the melted sauce smooth and cohesive. There was more, however. An additional secret ingredient! Instead of standard breadcrumbs, Reid tops the dish with crushed cornflakes mixed with melted butter. The crispy cereal topping adds a golden crunch that feels wonderfully unexpected. Paired with a butter-and-flour roux, warm milk and cream, and seasonings, the dish brings serious comfort, and Reid’s family and friends quickly devour it . When Torre and Chang cooked it up for a taste test, the flavors won them over. Even a world-class chef had to admit the cornflake twist worked. Bringing a football legend’s feast to your table After years of speculation, home cooks can finally try the full recipe for themselves. It takes a little prep work, especially grating all those different cheeses. Still, the payoff is a rich, bubbly pan built for big holiday gatherings. Whether you make it straight from Reid’s notes or add your own spin, someone finally solves the mystery . Thanksgiving tables everywhere just got a lot cheesier. The post Andy Reid’s legendary secret mac-n-cheese recipe has finally been shared with the world appeared first on Upworthy .

Η τραγουδίστρια, Brenda Lee, ήταν μόλις δύο ετών όταν ηχογράφησε το peren…
items.descriptionOriginal: Holiday season energy is officially here. Soon, the sounds of sleigh bells and Ho-ho-hoing Santas will fill every shopping center you walk into . And chances are good that you’ll hear the festive “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” pumping out of the mall’s speakers at least once. The singer, Brenda Lee, was only a tween when she recorded the perennial classic. Decades later, the song continues to climb the charts every December. Now it has earned a massive RIAA Diamond certification for surpassing 10 million copies . To mark the historic milestone, music superstar Taylor Swift surprised the 81-year-old legend in person. The heartwarming meetup brought Lee to tears. A heartfelt surprise between two music icons Seeing Taylor Swift present a gleaming Diamond plaque to Brenda Lee on behalf of the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) is a true gift to music fans. The song is an enduring holiday classic for sure, but there are even deeper connections between Swift and Lee. They both started young and began their recording careers in Tennessee. Swift’s debut album arrived when she turned 16 , while Lee was only 12. There’s plenty about this musician meet-cute that will bring a smile to your face. Especially Lee’s adorable astonishment at Taylor Swift’s height. When wearing heels, Swift is six feet tall. But the real emotion comes after Brenda Lee receives the Diamond Certification. She tears up as she mentions the song’s writer, Johnny Marks . You probably know his two other seasonal classics, “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” and “A Holly Jolly Christmas.” The song reached #1 on the Billboard charts again in 2023 . That made her the oldest woman to ever reach the top spot. “This is yours now, and it will be yours forever,” Swift tells an emotional Lee. Taylor also refers to Lee as “the original queen of Christmas.” Only one modern Christmas song reached Diamond status before “Rockin’…” That being Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Brenda Lee’s remarkable rise and holiday chart magic Brenda Lee’s story makes this milestone even more extraordinary . As a young child, she possessed a powerhouse voice. She only began singing professionally, however, after the death of her father. Lee sang at county fairs and on local TV to help earn money for her family. Soon after, she signed a record deal at Decca at 12 years old. Known affectionately as “Little Miss Dynamite,” Lee broke through in the late 1950s. She moved effortlessly between rockabilly, pop, and country music long before genre lines blurred. Her vocal grit and emotional maturity stunned listeners. Songs like “I’m Sorry” cemented her place as an unforgettable vocal force. Lee was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1997 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2002. Meanwhile, “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” is an annual chart phenomenon. Modern Billboard rules count both classic catalog songs and holiday tracks. And since streaming and radio play surge every winter, old favorites can suddenly sprint back toward No. 1 during peak holiday weeks. In Lee’s case, Spotify announced in 2024 that “Rockin’…” had crossed the one billion stream mark in 2024. Why this timeless classic still warms our hearts Music has a unique ability to freeze moments in time. A familiar guitar riff or joyful lyric can transport us straight back to a Christmas of your childhood. Lee’s song is part of a trio of tracks that were the first to merge holiday music with rock and roll beats . Bobby Helm’s “Jingle Bell Rock” came out of the gate swinging in 1957. That was followed the next year by Lee’s “Rockin’…” and Chuck Berry’s “Run Rudolph Run” —which leapt quickly onto the charts. It’s a seasonal formula that many of today’s recording artists try to replicate. Just this year, Olivia Rodrigo made a splash with “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” which evokes the New Wave sound of The Waitresses’ 1981 classic, “Christmas Wrapping.” What will always make Brenda Lee’s track so catchy is her youthful energy. Watching Taylor Swift honor such a trailblazer reminds us of what we love about the season. Family, friends, and holiday traditions set to a rockin’ beat for generations to come. The post Taylor Swift surprises 81-year-old Brenda Lee with RIAA Diamond plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: For many decades, Americans have debated Thanksgiving and the “first Thanksgiving” story, digging into the history versus the mythology of the Pilgrims and Native Americans breaking bread together. Some even shun the holiday to protest how the Thanksgiving origin story has been sanitized to obscure painful historical realities. The problem is that that hotly debated history is a myth within another myth, as the federal Thanksgiving holiday wasn’t originally tied to the Pilgrims, Native Americans, or Plymouth at all. Let’s unpack it. The first presidential Thanksgiving proclamation had zero mention of the Pilgrims Local Thanksgiving festivals had been observed in the U.S. long before it became a national holiday, often to give thanks for a successful harvest. But the official holiday is an entirely different thing. The first federal U.S. Thanksgiving holiday was proclaimed by George Washington in October of 1789 (which you can read here ). None of its over 450 words mention, or even allude to, the Pilgrims sitting down to feast with the Wampanoag people. Instead, Washington declared Thursday, November 26th, a holiday to give “sincere and humble thanks” to “that great and glorious Being, who is the beneficent Author of all the good that was, that is, or that will be” for bounties including the outcome of the Revolutionary War, the establishment of a constitutional government, the “civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed,” the ability to acquire knowledge, and the general blessings and favors of God. He also called for prayers asking God to pardon transgressions and bless the nation and all mankind. Nothing about the “first Thanksgiving” or anything related to that story. Lincoln made Thanksgiving an annual holiday. He also made no mention of the Pilgrims. Thanksgiving became an annual federal holiday with Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation naming the last Thursday in November an official day of Thanksgiving. The nation was in the middle of the Civil War, and Lincoln’s Thanksgiving proclamation spoke of the many things that were going well in the United States despite the ongoing military conflict. Something deeply moving about Lincoln making Thanksgiving a national holiday in the midst of the Civil War because we may “expect continuance of years with large increase of freedom” and “God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy.” pic.twitter.com/j5oFyPNeac — Phil Klay (@PhilKlay) November 25, 2025 “No human counsel hath devised nor hath any mortal hand worked out these great things,” the proclamation read. “They are the gracious gifts of the Most High God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy. It has seemed to me fit and proper that they should be solemnly, reverently and gratefully acknowledged as with one heart and one voice by the whole American People.” Lincoln also called for Americans to pray for the loved ones of those lost in the war, and to implore the Almighty “to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with the Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquillity and Union.” But again, nothing about Pilgrims or Native Americans or Plymouth. Lincoln created Thanksgiving to unite the U.S. during its bloodiest war. (In fact, Southerners resisted the Thanksgiving holiday , seeing it as Yankee abolitionist propaganda.) No president associated the Pilgrims with Thanksgiving until 1939—and that was just a brief mention Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving to the fourth Thursday of November instead of the last in 1939, when the last Thursday of November fell on the 30th, which created a late start to the holiday shopping season. Congress took the president’s lead and issued a resolution in 1941 , establishing the holiday as we know it today, on the fourth Thursday. In 1939, FDR moved Thanksgiving to the second to last Thursday of November. However, 16 states refused to accept the proclamation. It wasn't until Congress passed a resolution in 1941 that all states celebrated Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November. #Thanksgiving pic.twitter.com/JH7ifGtkr5 — American History TV (@cspanhistory) November 24, 2022 FDR’s 1939 Thanksgiving proclamation was the first to mention the Pilgrims, but even then, it wasn’t tied to any Pilgrim-Native “first Thanksgiving” meal. “More than three centuries ago at the season of the gathering in of the harvest, the Pilgrims humbly paused in their work and gave thanks to God for the preservation of their community and for the abundant yield of the soil,” FDR said. That’s it. That was the first official Pilgrim connection to the federal Thanksgiving holiday, and it came nearly six decades after it was established. So how did we end up with the ‘first Thanksgiving’ story and subsequent myth-busting? The tying of Thanksgiving to the image of a friendly feast between the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag (ignoring the complicated reality and history that followed) evolved primarily after the federal holiday was established. Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of the popular women’s periodical Godey Lady’s Book from 1837 until 1877, had made a relentless push for a national Thanksgiving holiday, petitioning five presidents before Lincoln finally made it happen. She called it a “good old puritan custom” in her pitch to make it a holiday, but she envisioned more of a Christian day of prayer rather than a big celebratory food feast. She did offer recipes for seasonal foods such as turkey and cranberry sauce, however, and her connecting the holiday to New England history and traditions planted the seed for modern Thanksgiving mythology. The widespread tie-in to the “first Thanksgiving” between the Pilgrims and Native Americans was driven largely by panic over immigration in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. People were worried about assimilation as a wave of immigrants arrived in the U.S., and a narrative of American identity emerged through a revised origin of the Thanksgiving holiday. As the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History writes, “The holiday was secularized during the last decades of the [19th] century, and by the twentieth century, costumed festivals honoring the Pilgrims became themes of elaborate grade-school pageants—an effective way to ‘Americanize’ immigrants. These annual activities showcased Puritan values and Yankee customs, promoting civic folk rituals.” Since then, it’s stuck. The history of colonists and indigenous peoples is important—it’s just not what Thanksgiving was about The way the story of Thanksgiving has played out has led to woeful inaccuracies and painful erasures of indigenous people’s experiences in American history. Because of that, the fact that the national Thanksgiving holiday wasn’t even based on that story adds yet another layer of complexity to conversations around celebrating it. On one hand, it means we can honestly make the holiday broadly about gratitude, as the original federal proclamations did. On the other hand, discussions of the historical inaccuracies surrounding the “first Thanksgiving” have been, and continue to be, important. Nothing about correcting the record on the official federal holiday origin erases the need for those conversations. In fact, it’s a good reminder that they need to be had regularly, not just once a year on a holiday whose origin has been muddled in so many ways. The post The origin of the Thanksgiving holiday actually had nothing to do with the Pilgrims or Native Americans appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Tattoos have become as American as apple pie. But it turns out they still make people nervous.
items.description: Αν γυρίσατε τον χρόνο πίσω στη δεκαετία του 1980, μια από τις μεγαλύτερες αλλαγές που θα παρατηρούσατε είναι η έλλειψη τατουάζ. Υπολογίζεται ότι στη δεκαετία του '80, περίπου το 10% του αμερικανικού πληθυσμού ήταν ραμμένο, σε σύγκριση με το 32% σήμερα. Η κοινή γνώμη άρχισε να αλλάζει τη δεκαετία του 1990, καθώς οι εναλλακτικές και πανκ ροκ υποκουλτούρες έπληξαν το mainstream και ακόμη και τους στρέιτ φολκ σταρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you went back in time to the 1980s , one of the biggest changes you’d notice is the lack of tattoos. It’s estimated that in the ’80s, around 10% of the American population was tatted, as compared to 32% today. Public opinion began to shift in the 1990s as alternative and punk rock subcultures hit the mainstream and even straight-laced folks started getting inked. In the ‘90s, tattoos shifted from a symbol of gangs, the military, or dangerous subcultures to an art form, with the rise of superstar tattoo artists such as Ed Hardy and Mr. Cartoon . Another big cultural shift during this time was that women made up a large number of those embracing the new body aesthetic. Tattoos have reached the mainstream, and visible ink is now acceptable in many professions where it used to be forbidden, so these days, body art doesn’t seem intimidating. However, a new study by Farid Pazhoohi, Ph.D., published in Evolutionary Psychological Science found that tattoos still make people a little uncomfortable. Why We Might Give Tattooed Strangers a Little More Room | Farid Pazhoohi Ph D, Psychology Today New research finds that tattoos subtly shape comfort and attractiveness ratings. Picture two people standing in line ahead of you. They look identical, except that one has visible… pic.twitter.com/r2ZK5UGxMu — Owen Gregorian (@OwenGregorian) November 21, 2026 In the study, people were shown computer-generated images of people with or without tattoos, and they found that those without tattoos made them more comfortable. “People generally felt slightly more comfortable with the non-tattooed figures than with their tattooed counterparts,” Pazhoohi wrote in Psychology Today . “The average comfort ratings were approximately 5.12 versus 4.95 on a seven-point scale. The difference was small but statistically significant, and it appeared for both male and female figures.” It’s interesting that some are still uncomfortable around people with tattoos, given how prevalent they are. But it’s good news for those who got inked to look edgier and more intimidating—your body art still works on some people. A tattoo artist doing their job. Credit: Canva The study found that for those who are intimidated, it doesn’t matter how close the person is to them. “Although participants felt more comfortable as the distance increased, the effect of tattoos did not significantly change with distance,” Pazhoohi wrote. “This suggests that tattoos may influence our general impression of someone rather than specifically making us uncomfortable when that person gets too close.” Another interesting takeaway is that the study found men and women have differing opinions on whether tattoos make someone more attractive. “Male participants rated both male and female figures as more attractive when they did not have tattoos. Female participants, however, showed no significant difference in attractiveness ratings between tattooed and non-tattooed figures,” Pazhoohi continues. A woman getting a ttoo on her thigh. Credit: Canva Ultimately, the study shows that even though tattoos have become nearly ubiquitous in modern society, they can still affect how we perceive others without knowing anything else about them. “What I find particularly interesting is that participants knew nothing about the figures they were judging. They had no information about their personalities, backgrounds, or behaviour,” Pazhoohi wrote. “Yet changing one visible feature was enough to influence their ratings. It is a small example of something much broader: how readily we form impressions of others based on appearance, often without knowing why.” The post Tattoos have become as American as apple pie. But it turns out they still make people nervous. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Πριν από εξήντα χρόνια, οι Monkees κυκλοφόρησαν το "I'm a Believer", το οποίο έγινε η μεγαλύτερη επιτυχία του γκρουπ, περνώντας αξιοσημείωτες επτά συνεχόμενες εβδομάδες στην κορυφή του Billboard Hot 100. Και φυσικά, εκτός από το μουσικό ταλέντο, το συγκρότημα είχε σίγουρα τον Neil Diamond να ευχαριστήσει, αφού έγραψε το τραγούδι. Μόνο ο Diamond αρχικά οραματίστηκε έναν πολύ διαφορετικό τραγουδιστή να το φέρει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sixty years ago, The Monkees released “I’m a Believer,” which became the group’s biggest hit, spending a remarkable seven consecutive weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100. And of course, musical talent aside, the band certainly had Neil Diamond to thank, since he wrote the song. Only Diamond originally envisioned a much different singer to bring the song to life. “I’m a Believer”…as a country song? In 1966, Diamond was in New York, on the precipice of a breakthrough as a solo songwriter, following the success of his single “Cherry, Cherry .” During this time, Diamond wrote “I’m a Believer,” which he considered for country music crooner Eddy Arnold, known for “Make the World Go Away.” Not exactly the upbeat, radio-friendly pop group The Monkees would become. However, music executive Don Kirshner steered the song to The Monkees instead, with Micky Dolenz singing lead vocals and Jeff Barry as the producer. And the timing of that decision couldn’t have worked out any better. When “I’m a Believer” was released, the Monkees’ self-titled sitcom premiered on NBC, and their debut single, “Last Train to Clarksville,” had reached No. 1 on the Hot 100. The Monkees had a pretty incredible run with it “I’m a Believer” quickly became one of the defining songs of the decade and helped establish The Monkees as something much bigger than a fictional band created for television. Not to mention, it became one of Diamond’s most celebrated songwriting achievements. A win-win all around. But the song’s story didn’t end with the 1960s. Diamond eventually recorded his own version in 1971, and other artists have put their own spins on the song over the years. Then Smash Mouth gave it another life One of its biggest second lives came in 2001, when Smash Mouth recorded “I’m a Believer” for the soundtrack to Shrek . Their version reached No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100, giving the 35-year-old song another run on the charts. The cover became one of the most recognizable musical moments from the movie, helping cement Smash Mouth’s version alongside The Monkees’ original in pop culture. For younger listeners, the song suddenly had a whole new context, one that had nothing to do with a 1960s sitcom. Dolenz looks back on “I’m a Believer” 60 years later In celebration of the song’s 60th anniversary, Dolenz, the last surviving member of The Monkees, shared a heartfelt Instagram tribute commending the various artists who came together to bring it to life. View this post on Instagram “A lot of wonderful people helped create that sound. Stan Free played the unmistakable organ part, Artie Butler handled the arrangement, and Neil himself played acoustic guitar on the session.” Dolenz also reflected on what the song has meant to him after performing it countless times over the years. “I’ve sung that song more times than I could ever count, and it still means a great deal to me. It’s the song we close every show with, and there’s something incredibly special about hearing a whole room sing it back. No matter where we play, that moment always gets me,” he added. “If you’re lucky, a few songs become part of your life. For me, ‘I’m a Believer’ is one of those.” The post Neil Diamond wrote The Monkees’ biggest hit, but they weren’t his first choice to sing it appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Solar panels are designed to absorb most of the incident light. Only part of the absorbed light is converted into electricity; the rest excites vibrations in the crystal lattice, which means it is converted into heat. An ideal heat shield for solar cells should reflect the unusable infrared components of the incident light while, at the same time, allowing all components of the light spectrum that can be converted into electrical energy to pass.

items.descriptionOriginal: A new approach for designing cathode materials that could help enhance cycle performance has been proposed. A research team led by professor Kisuk Kang of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at Seoul National University College of Engineering has identified a principle for suppressing voltage decay through the arrangement of atomic layers in cathode materials. Through experiments and simulations, the researchers found that an "O6 structure," which combines characteristics of different atomic arrangements, reduces structural evolution within the material during cycles.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How to Reduce Waste When Renovating Your Home Reading Time: 3 minutes Renovating can make your home work better for you, but stripping out rooms and replacing old materials can create a lot of waste along the way. In England alone, 63.3 million tonnes of non-hazardous construction and demolition waste were generated in 2024, according to UK statistics on waste . Your individual renovation will only represent a tiny part of that picture, but it still makes sense to question what you throw away. Keeping useful features, finding new homes for unwanted materials and buying with longevity in mind can all make a refurbishment less wasteful. Work with what you already have A renovation does not have to start with an empty room. Before removing anything, look at what you already have and decide whether each feature genuinely needs replacing or simply needs some attention. Kitchen units offer a good example. If the carcasses remain sturdy, you could keep them and change the doors or handles instead. Wooden flooring can often be sanded and refinished, while dated furniture may look completely different after a repair or a fresh coat of paint. Keeping existing features can make financial sense too. When you avoid unnecessarily replacing a perfectly usable item, you can put that part of your budget towards improvements that matter more to you. It also helps to separate function from appearance. Something may no longer suit the style you have in mind, but that does not necessarily make it waste. Painting or repairing it could achieve the result you want without buying a brand-new replacement. Find another use for what you remove You will not be able to keep everything, particularly during a larger renovation. However, removing an item from your home does not automatically mean you need to put it in a skip. Doors, cabinets, shelves and unopened building materials could potentially find a second home. You might sell suitable pieces through Facebook Marketplace or eBay, offer them through Freecycle, or contact a local reclamation yard to see what it accepts. Think about this before demolition begins. Once someone throws reusable materials into a skip alongside rubble and broken plasterboard, you may find it much harder to recover them in a usable condition. You can also keep certain leftover materials for future repairs. A few spare bathroom tiles take up very little storage space, for example, but could prove useful if one cracks several years after you finish the renovation. The same applies to a small amount of correctly labelled paint or spare flooring. Be selective about what you replace Sometimes replacing an old fitting is unavoidable. It may leak, perform poorly or simply have reached the end of its useful life. However, renovating gives you an opportunity to think more carefully about what genuinely needs to go. In a kitchen, you might replace damaged worktops while keeping a perfectly usable sink, or change cupboard fronts without removing the units behind them. If you do need new kitchen taps , choosing a style that works with the finished room can sit alongside practical considerations such as water efficiency and build quality. You can use the same thinking throughout your home. A higher-quality fitting that you can maintain or repair may stay in place considerably longer than a cheaper alternative that you have to replace when one component fails. Try to consider the expected lifespan of an item alongside its upfront price. Spending a little more on something durable may reduce the number of times you need to buy, remove and dispose of the same type of product in the future. Avoid creating waste with new materials Renovation waste does not only come from old materials. Ordering too much of something can leave you with boxes of tiles, excess timber or unused flooring once the work finishes. Measure the space carefully before ordering and calculate how much material the project realistically requires. You will usually need to allow some extra for cuts, breakages and mistakes, but that is different from ordering a large surplus simply to be safe. It is worth checking a retailer’s returns policy before you buy as well. If it accepts unused full packs, you have the option of returning excess materials rather than storing them indefinitely or throwing them away. You may also find ways to use smaller leftovers around the home. Timber offcuts could become a shelf, while a handful of spare tiles might be enough for a small splashback or another repair. Creating a more sustainable home is not only about adding new eco-friendly products . Sometimes the greener decision is to keep something for longer, repair what you can and think about where materials will end up before you remove them. With a little more planning, you can still create a home that feels different without treating everything that came before as disposable. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work Reading Time: 4 minutes How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work There are more than 100 million annual bird sightings logged on eBird by observers every day, yet many nature enthusiasts still assume meaningful conservation work requires formal lab credentials and massive institutional budgets. A lingering gap between public curiosity and formal scientific access often leaves local ecosystems unmonitored for years. Citizen science bridges that divide by turning routine outdoor observations into structured ecological data. Worldwide, conservation agencies, universities, and wildlife nonprofits now actively recruit everyday observers to track species shifts, flag habitat loss, and expand research capacity far beyond what small field teams could manage alone. What Citizen Science Is and Why It Matters Citizen science invites members of the public to collect, classify, and share real-world observations with professional researchers. Rather than replacing trained ecologists, public contributors act as an expansive sensory network across neighborhoods, coastlines, and rural landscapes. Small academic teams rarely have the budget to monitor thousands of square miles simultaneously. Volunteers fill those geographic and seasonal blind spots simply by documenting what lives in their backyards or along familiar trails. Even a single timestamped photograph of a blooming wildflower or migrating raptor adds an anchor point to regional biodiversity maps. How Volunteer Data Informs Habitat Protection and Species Management Raw sightings only become useful when researchers can aggregate them into clear ecological patterns. Once uploaded to shared repositories, thousands of individual logs reveal when migratory birds arrive early, where invasive plants are spreading, or which amphibian populations are quietly declining. Wildlife managers rely on these trends to prioritize land acquisition and adjust seasonal protections. Here’s an example. When volunteer records consistently show pollinators clustering along a specific utility corridor, municipal planners gain concrete evidence to preserve that strip instead of mowing it down. Accurate local records turn vague environmental concern into defensible policy decisions. Turning Field Curiosity into a Conservation Career Spending weekends logging water quality or tracking nesting shorebirds frequently changes how people view their own professional lives. Casual curiosity sharpens into methodical questioning once an observer starts noticing why certain species thrive in one creek and vanish from the next. Many volunteers discover they want more than a weekend hobby. Moving from enthusiast to full-time practitioner usually requires structured academic preparation. Inspired participants explore options ranging from technical field certifications to formal biology degree programs that build the scientific foundation needed for careers in wildlife research, environmental policy, and conservation management. Coursework in ecology, genetics, and statistical analysis equips aspiring conservationists to design the very studies they once supported as volunteers. Partnering with Schools, Nonprofits, and Conservation Organizations Individual data collection carries real weight, yet institutional partnerships multiply what a single observer can accomplish. Local schools, land trusts, and watershed coalitions frequently coordinate regional monitoring drives that align volunteer effort with urgent research gaps. Community groups can amplify their conservation footprint through several collaborative pathways: K-12 classrooms adopt nearby streams to submit seasonal macroinvertebrate counts to state environmental agencies Regional land trusts pair amateur naturalists with staff biologists for annual breeding bird inventories Municipal park departments host weekend BioBlitz events to catalog urban tree health and insect diversity University extension offices train community volunteers to monitor invasive species along public trail systems Working inside an organized network ensures that observations follow standardized protocols, making the resulting datasets far more reliable for peer-reviewed analysis. How Community Involvement Builds Local Stewardship People rarely fight to protect landscapes they barely know. Regularly surveying a neighborhood wetland or coastal dune creates an intimate familiarity that abstract news headlines never match. Once residents recognize individual warbler species or spot early signs of soil erosion, conservation stops feeling like someone else’s responsibility. Neighbors begin attending zoning hearings, advocating for native landscaping, and mentoring younger observers. Shared fieldwork transforms passive bystanders into vocal stewards who hold local leaders accountable for environmental decisions. Popular Citizen Science Projects and Monitoring Tools Getting involved does not require specialized laboratory equipment or remote expedition travel. Modern mobile platforms and long-running seasonal counts make participation accessible from almost anywhere. Birdwatchers frequently contribute to global avian databases during annual backyard counts, logging species abundance across winter and spring migrations. Pollinator enthusiasts use dedicated survey protocols to record bumblebee and monarch activity in community gardens. Meanwhile, smartphone wildlife apps allow hikers to snap photos of butterflies , fungi, reptiles, and plants, using computer vision paired with community verification to confirm the identities of species within hours. Measuring Long-Term Conservation Impact Skeptics sometimes wonder whether crowd-sourced observations hold up under rigorous scientific scrutiny. Over the past decade, researchers have developed robust validation frameworks that filter outliers and verify identification accuracy. Recent evaluations show that adaptable volunteer monitoring protocols help conservation scientists respond quickly to shifting ecological priorities without sacrificing data integrity. In marine and coastal regions, international bodies have also established clear quality labeling and sharing standards so community-gathered ocean datasets integrate smoothly into global climate assessments. Longitudinal records spanning ten or twenty years now underpin major habitat restoration grants and endangered species reviews. Getting Started in Your Local Community Stepping into citizen science works best when you start small and stay consistent. Choose a single taxon or local habitat you already enjoy visiting, then commit to observing it across changing seasons. Researchers consistently find that structured community-based biodiversity monitoring yields the strongest conservation value when participants stick with simple, repeatable reporting routines. Choosing a Local Focus Area Start with a nearby park, creek, or backyard garden rather than planning ambitious weekend expeditions. Familiarity with one small patch makes it much easier to spot subtle ecological shifts over time. Learning Basic Observation Protocols Spend twenty minutes reviewing how a project records location, weather, and species counts before submitting your first entry. Clean metadata matters just as much as a sharp photograph when scientists analyze your logs later. Connecting with Regional Coordinators Reach out to a local nature center, watershed alliance, or birding club to ask which datasets regional managers actually need. Aligning your walks with active local priorities ensures your notes solve real conservation problems. Where Everyday Observation Meets Lasting Stewardship Citizen science proves that meaningful environmental protection does not belong exclusively to credentialed specialists. Every careful observation adds another verifiable thread to our collective understanding of changing ecosystems. Whether you stay an active neighborhood volunteer or pursue formal scientific training, consistent attention to the natural world creates tangible momentum for conservation. If this piece was helpful, explore more guides on environmental conservation, field research, and community stewardship across our related articles below. The post How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work appeared first on Happy Eco News .
