Το καθήκον της είναι να διασφαλίσει ότι κανείς δεν κόβει δέντρα, δεν βλάπτει τη βλάστηση ή δεν επιτρέπει στα βοοειδή να βόσκουν εκεί που δεν πρέπει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every morning, 75-year-old Bhagirathi Devi walks into the forest beside her village in Uttarakhand's Champawat district. She patrols the area, returns home around noon and heads back for another round at 2 pm, often staying until sunset. Her task is to ensure that nobody cuts trees, damages vegetation or allows cattle to graze where they should not. For more than two decades, Bhagirathi has helped protect and restore this forest in Manar village. Known locally as Van Amma, she began the effort in 2000, when the woodland had become almost barren following years of excessive grazing and tree felling. Today, the community-managed forest is also a site of fire prevention. In a report published by Down To Earth on 31 May 2025, journalist Bhagirath documented how the village's women organised themselves to restore the forest, regulate access, and remove dry leaves and pine needles before the fire season. According to residents, there has been no forest fire in the restored forest since the initiative began. The Champawat Forest Department has also recognised the effort as a model for fire prevention. Manar's experience points to something important about forest protection in Uttarakhand: preventing fires is not always about reaching a burning hillside with firefighting equipment. It can begin much earlier, with people who understand the forest, depend on it and have the authority to regulate how it is used. Across the state's mountain villages, women are increasingly taking on this responsibility. As men migrate in search of employment, women remain to manage agriculture, livestock and household needs. Their daily work brings them into close contact with forests, making them among the first to notice smoke and respond to small fires. The Ghost Village question: who is left to protect the forest? Uttarakhand's migration story is often told through the image of the ghost village: a settlement where houses remain locked, agricultural fields lie fallow, and only a handful of residents remain. The scale of depopulation is reflected in government figures cited in the 2021 report Locked Houses, Fallow Lands: Climate Change and Migration in Uttarakhand, India , prepared by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. According to the 2011 Census, 1,048 of Uttarakhand's 16,793 revenue villages were uninhabited. A subsequent survey by the state's Rural Development and Migration Commission in 2018 identified another 734 villages that had become uninhabited after 2011. The report notes that depopulation has affected all 13 districts, although the problem is more pronounced in the hill districts. However, not every village affected by migration is entirely deserted. In many settlements, men have moved to towns and cities for work while women, children and older residents remain. Women continue cultivating fields, looking after cattle, collecting forest produce and caring for family members. This changes who is available to respond when a forest fire breaks out. In Manar, Bhagirathi Devi's initiative began with a problem familiar to many women in mountain villages. Before the forest was restored, women had to walk seven to eight kilometres to a neighbouring forest, Siddhmandir, to collect fodder and firewood. Bhagirathi told Down To Earth that this journey took five to six hours every day. The loss of nearby forest cover had also affected the flow of local springs. Restoring the woodland was therefore not simply a conservation exercise. It was an attempt to make village life more sustainable. For women who remain, the responsibility is consequently twofold: maintaining households in villages with fewer working-age residents and protecting the natural resources that make those settlements habitable. Why women are often the first to notice a fire The reasons women become first responders are closely connected to the division of labour in rural households. Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. These activities keep them in and around forests for several hours a day. When a fire begins, they may notice the first signs of smoke before it becomes visible from the village or reaches the attention of forest officials. A 2023 paper by researchers Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R C Sundriyal, Jeet Ram and Surendra P Singh, published in Tropical Ecology , provides important context for understanding this relationship. Titled Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya , the research analysed satellite-derived fire data from 2002 to 2020 across 24 forest divisions in the state. Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. Photograph: (TBI-File picture) The researchers recorded 80,440 fire detections over the 19 years. Their analysis found that warmer pre-monsoon temperatures, a greater proportion of chir pine forest and lower winter and pre-monsoon rainfall together explained 56% of the variation in fire incidence. They also noted that human activities associated with farming and the collection of fuel and fodder influence the likelihood of fires. The paper specifically recommends examining changes in population distribution and communities' dependence on forests as part of effective fire management. This is where women's everyday relationship with forests becomes relevant. They are not simply residents living near a fire-prone landscape. Their livelihoods are directly connected to the condition of that landscape. A fire can mean losing fodder for cattle, travelling farther to collect fuelwood, spending additional hours searching for forest produce and, in some cases, losing agricultural resources. The relationship between gender and firefighting is not simply a question of who is more willing to respond. It is also a question of who is expected to undertake the work when the forest that sustains the household is threatened. In a report published by Mongabay on 8 September 2026, journalist Swati Thapa documented this pattern in Uttarakhand villages. Researcher Kavya Pandey of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bengaluru, told Thapa that traditional gender roles and women's responsibility for household work and caregiving help explain why they are often the first to respond to fires. This offers a field-level account of a wider connection between women's labour and forest protection. How a community can stop a fire before it spreads Manar offers a particularly useful example of what happens when women move beyond responding to individual fires and take responsibility for managing an entire forest. When Bhagirathi Devi began the initiative in 2000, she brought other women together to form a van panchayat, a community forest-management council. She was unanimously elected its first sarpanch. The initial work involved clearing and fencing parts of the degraded forest. The women also worked with BAIF Development Research Foundation, a Pune-based organisation involved in silvopasture initiatives in the region. Silvopasture combines trees, grasses and livestock management . The idea was to restore vegetation while ensuring that the community could continue to access fodder and other forest resources. With BAIF's support and training, residents fenced the woodland using stones and thorny plants. They cleared invasive species such as lantana and planted native trees and fodder species, including banj oak ( Quercus leucotrichophora ), angu ( Fraxinus micrantha ) and utish ( Alnus nepalensis ). For two years, grazing was prohibited to allow the vegetation to recover. It took another five to six years for the trees to establish themselves. According to Manju Manral, the first president of Manar's Silvopasture Management Committee, 11.6 hectares of forest were eventually revived. The work was not entirely voluntary. Down To Earth reported that women involved in the restoration received Rs 120 per day from BAIF. They voluntarily contributed 10% of their wages towards maintaining the forest. Each household also contributed Rs 20 a month towards Bhagirathi's salary for guarding the woodland. A separate 2022 field study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, BAIF and the Centre for Ecology Development and Research also found that the forest under Manar's van panchayat was healthier than the forest outside its management area. What the 2026 fire season reveals In an assessment published on 2 June 2026 on the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's (IIRS) Sudoor Manthan science portal , researchers Athira V Mukundan, Madhusmita Murmu, Chandra Mohan Bhatt and Arijit Roy analysed forest-fire activity across the state between January and May 2026. Using NASA's MODIS active-fire data, they recorded: January: 200 active-fire detections. February: 113 detections. March: 178 detections. April: 207 detections. May: 433 detections. The May figure represented a 109% increase over April. It also accounted for approximately 38% of all detections recorded between January and May. Pauri Garhwal recorded the highest cumulative number of detections during the five-month period, at 207, followed by Chamoli with 190 and Tehri Garhwal with 130. District level of fire detections in May, 2026 Photograph: (FIRMS, NASA via Indian Institute of Remote Sensing) The researchers also used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to map burned areas in Pauri Garhwal. Comparing images from April with those captured between 25 and 28 May, they identified approximately 838.66 sq km of burned area. Most of this was classified as low-severity burning, while 0.94 sq km fell into the highest severity category. These figures are satellite-based detections and mapped burn areas, not a count of independently verified individual fires. Nevertheless, they show how quickly fire activity intensified towards the end of the pre-monsoon season. The 2023 research by Singh and his colleagues helps explain this seasonal pattern. Most fires in Uttarakhand occur between March and May, when temperatures rise, vegetation dries and fresh pine litter accumulates on the forest floor. The human cost of these fires can be severe. On 13 June 2024, four forest department personnel died while fighting a blaze in Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary in Almora district. According to a report by The Times of India on 14 June 2024, four others were seriously injured after the firefighting team was engulfed by flames. For women who fight smaller fires in community forests, the risks are no less real, particularly when they have no protective clothing, footwear or firefighting equipment. Besides, women's participation does not automatically translate into decision-making power. A 2026 research chapter by K Nagahama, published in Springer Proceedings in Earth and Environmental Sciences , examines women's participation in a Uttarakhand van panchayat through household surveys, interviews, forest surveys and long-term observations conducted between 2011 and 2023. The research examines an important distinction: being present in community forest management does not necessarily mean having equal authority over decisions or control over resources. The problem is also visible in the reporting from Uttarakhand. The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. Photograph: (TBI-File Picture) In her September 2026 Mongabay investigation, Swati Thapa spoke to Laxmi Kharayat, a field trainer with The Hunger Project, who described cases where women formally listed as van panchayat heads were unaware of their positions, while male family members exercised authority on their behalf. There is also a gap between the work women undertake and the employment opportunities available to them. Seasonal fire watchers recruited by the forest department are predominantly men. Women who assist in firefighting often do so without regular wages or access to appropriate protective equipment. The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. The challenge is to ensure that these provisions translate into practical support for women at the village level. This means providing women with training in fire prevention and safe firefighting, protective clothing, gloves, sturdy footwear, communication equipment and access to emergency assistance. It also means creating paid opportunities for women as seasonal fire watchers and ensuring that they have actual decision-making authority within van panchayats. Just as importantly, their work should not be treated as an unpaid extension of household responsibilities simply because they are the people who remain in the village. Forest protection begins with the people who depend on it Bhagirathi Devi's work did not begin with a firefighting operation. It began with a forest that had become too degraded to support the people living beside it. By bringing women together, restoring native vegetation, regulating grazing and establishing a system for removing dry litter, the village created a model of long-term community protection. For women in Uttarakhand's mountain villages, protecting a forest also means protecting the resources that keep their households functioning. When the forest burns, the consequences reach their cattle, farms, water sources and daily routines. Their leadership has shown that communities can play a significant role in preventing fires, provided they have the authority and resources to do so. The next step is to ensure that this responsibility does not remain invisible or unpaid. The women who recognise the first signs of smoke, organise their neighbours and maintain village forests should be treated as essential partners in forest protection, not as an informal firefighting force expected to manage with whatever tools they have at hand. Sources: 'Guardians of groves-How women of an Uttarakhand village successfully revived a lost forest' : By Bhagirath, Published on 31 May 2025 'How Uttarakhand's women and villages are defending forests with community, care and smart tools' : By Varsha Singh, Published on 16 June 2025 'Forest commons for multiple benefits: Restoration of degraded land and revival of springs in Uttarakhand, India' : By Dinesh Prasad Raturi, Santosh Paudel & Erica Udas, Published on 14 October 2022 'Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial, and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya' : By Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R. items.descriptionOriginal: Different pathways to net zero greenhouse gas emissions could have wildly different effects on other parts of the natural environment, according to a new study. “How we decarbonize may matter just as much as how ambitious our climate goals are,” says study team member Alvaro Hahn Menacho , a PhD candidate at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Zurich, Switzerland. Until now, most research on net-zero pathways has focused on cost and greenhouse gas emissions. Some studies have looked at the broader environmental context at a national level, but never at a global scale. The new work provides an opportunity to get a clearer picture of the tradeoffs involved before decarbonization infrastructure is locked into place, Hahn Menacho and his colleagues say. The researchers analyzed 24 different climate change mitigation pathways from three existing large-scale modeling efforts. The pathways involve a range of socioeconomic development patterns (for example, will population growth be high, or more modest?), climate ambition ( will the world decarbonize fast, or slowly? ), and energy system specifics (will the green transition involve a lot of wind and solar power, or a lot of bioenergy with carbon capture?). They assessed these scenarios with a life cycle analysis using a new open-source software tool, also developed at PSI, that enabled them to compare the future impact of the pathways on human health, both;} Recommended Reading: The overlooked wiring problem in the clean-energy transition “Decarbonization brings substantial benefits beyond reducing greenhouse gas emissions, particularly for human health and ecosystem quality,” Hahn Menacho says. “However, it does not automatically reduce pressures on natural resources such as land, water, and minerals.” Moving away from fossil fuels could lead to anywhere between a 13% decrease and a 354% increase in land use by the energy system, the researchers found. That’s because this figure strongly depends on the use of biomass. Pathways that rely heavily on bioenergy will require a lot more land to grow biofuel crops. Similarly, a pathway that relies more on carbon capture to soak up ongoing emissions will require a larger energy system and impose higher burdens on various aspects of the environment than one that prioritizes preventing emissions in the first place – even if the result is a similar emissions balance overall. “One particularly interesting finding was that ambitious climate goals primarily accelerate the demand for critical minerals rather than substantially increasing their cumulative extraction over the century,” Hahn Menacho says. Critical minerals are substances like lithium, cobalt, and nickel that are needed for green technologies but involve supply chain risks due to their scarcity or limited distribution. The finding “suggests that delaying decarbonization does not necessarily solve the resource challenge,” he says. The researchers aim to take these global insights and drill back down “to develop more geographically detailed impact assessments,” Hahn Menacho says. Among other research priorities, “an important next step is better understanding where these environmental pressures occur and how they can be mitigated.” Source: Hahn Menacho A. items.descriptionOriginal: A borewell can run dry without much warning. For a farmer depending on it to irrigate crops or a family relying on it for everyday water needs, the question that follows is simple: how much water is actually left underground? Finding an answer is not easy. Unlike rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, groundwater reserves cannot be seen. Their availability depends on several factors, from rainfall and soil conditions to the rate at which water is extracted. Without reliable estimates, planning how much to draw or where to focus conservation efforts becomes difficult. By analysing historical borewell records, rainfall patterns and soil characteristics, JALAAKAR attempts to make underground water reserves easier to understand. Photograph: ( Firstpost ) A school student from Surat, Gujarat, is exploring how technology could make this information easier to access. Dheyay Shah has developed JALAAKAR, a machine-learning-based tool that estimates groundwater availability across different talukas using historical records and environmental data. His innovation recently won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026, a nationwide challenge that received more than 6,100 project submissions from school students across India. Making groundwater easier to understand India depends heavily on groundwater for drinking water, agriculture and other everyday needs. However, excessive extraction, changing rainfall patterns and growing demand have put pressure on these underground reserves. One of the difficulties in managing this resource is knowing how much water is available in a particular area. Groundwater levels can vary depending on local geography, the amount of rainfall received, and how much water is being extracted. This is where Dheyay's project comes in. Instead of relying on isolated measurements, JALAAKAR brings together different sources of information to generate estimates that help people better understand groundwater conditions. How JALAAKAR uses machine learning At its core, JALAAKAR uses machine learning to identify patterns in historical groundwater and environmental data. The tool considers information such as past borewell records, rainfall patterns, and soil characteristics. Each of these offers a different piece of information about underground water reserves. For instance, rainfall influences how much water can seep into the ground and replenish aquifers. Soil characteristics determine how readily this water can percolate, while borewell records provide insights into changes in groundwater levels over time. JALAAKAR analyses these datasets to identify relationships and recurring patterns. It then uses what it learns from the historical information to estimate groundwater availability at the taluka level. JALAAKAR uses historical data to identify patterns and estimate groundwater availability across different talukas. Photograph: ( Digit ) In simpler terms, the tool attempts to use what has happened in the past to understand what groundwater conditions might look like in a particular area. Such estimates could eventually help local communities, farmers, and those involved in water management make more informed decisions about extraction and conservation. However, predictive estimates are not a substitute for actual groundwater measurements. The tool's accuracy, independent field validation, and suitability for different geographical conditions would need to be established before it can be used for wider water-management decisions. A young innovator looking beneath the surface Dheyay's project was recognised at vivo Ignite 2026, where he emerged as the national winner. The competition brought together school students working on ideas that apply science and technology to real-world challenges. With more than 6,100 projects received, the challenge evaluated innovations on parameters such as creativity, scientific application, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and potential social impact. What makes JALAAKAR interesting is the problem it chooses to address. Groundwater management is often discussed in terms of large-scale infrastructure and policy, but it also begins with something much simpler: understanding how much water is available before using it. Dheyay's innovation won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026. Photograph: ( Tehelka ) Dheyay's work explores how data can help answer that question. While the tool would need further testing and refinement before wider application, it offers a promising starting point for making groundwater information more accessible. For a young student, looking beneath the surface has meant looking at a problem that affects millions of people. And if developed further, JALAAKAR could contribute to a future where communities have better information to guide how they use and protect one of their most important natural resources. Sources: 'Dheyay Shah named winner for Vivo Ignite 2026, over 6,100 projects received' by Economic Times, Published on 29 October 2026. 'Surat school student uses machine learning to estimate groundwater availability; project wins national innovation challenge' by Sanjay Sharma for The Times Of India, Published on 10 November 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: What comes to mind when you think of a successful business? Crores in revenue, thousands of employees, a presence across the world, or perhaps a celebrated CEO? Now consider a few other measures of success. How many women earned their first independent income? How many people with disabilities found a workplace where they could build a career? How many families could afford life-saving medical treatment? How many rural artisans could earn a living without leaving their villages? Recent conversations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's management practices have brought a larger question into focus: what truly makes a good business leader? Closer to home, these five Indian enterprises offer a different perspective on success. From hospitality and healthcare to waste management and handicrafts, they show how building a profitable business can go hand in hand with creating meaningful opportunities and improving people's lives. Making room for every ability At Lemon Tree Hotels, learning Indian Sign Language is part of employee training. It helps colleagues communicate with one another and makes everyday working life more accessible for employees with hearing disabilities. At Lemon Tree Hotels, employees learn Indian Sign Language to build a workplace where everyone can communicate and thrive. Photograph: ( Hotelier India ) Patu Keswani, the founder of the hotel group, began hiring people with disabilities in 2007. Over the years, the company has adapted its training programmes to accommodate people with different needs. Deaf employees receive training with the help of sign language interpreters, while colleagues with low vision are provided accessible learning materials. Some neurodivergent employees undergo internships lasting more than six months to help them settle into their roles. According to its 2025–26 annual report , Lemon Tree employed 305 people with disabilities and another 635 people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds across its owned, leased and managed hotels. Much like several inclusive caf s across India , the hotel chain demonstrates how adapting workplaces to people's needs can open up meaningful career opportunities. Taking village crafts to the world In 1978, Nand Kishore Chaudhary began Jaipur Rugs with two looms and nine artisans. He wanted to connect rural craftspeople directly with larger markets, helping them earn through skills they had developed over generations. Jaipur Rugs connects 40,000 artisans across 600 villages to global markets, creating livelihoods through generations-old weaving skills. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) According to the founder's website , the business has grown to work with around 40,000 artisans across 600 villages in five Indian states. Around 80 percent of them are women. For many of these women, weaving offers an opportunity to earn from their homes without having to migrate to cities or travel far for work. As The Better India previously reported , the company delivers raw materials to artisans' homes and collects the finished carpets from them. Through its Manchaha initiative, artisans also get the freedom to create their own rug designs, drawing inspiration from their surroundings, experiences and imagination. Their craftsmanship has found customers across the world while creating livelihood opportunities closer to home. Making life-saving surgeries affordable For a family struggling to afford heart surgery, the cost of treatment can stand between a loved one and potentially life-saving medical care. It was this challenge that cardiac surgeon Dr Devi Shetty sought to address when he founded Narayana Health in Bengaluru in 2001. Narayana Health's high-volume hospital model helps reduce treatment costs, making specialised cardiac care accessible to more families. Photograph: ( GovInsider ) His hospital model focuses on performing a large number of surgeries, making efficient use of medical equipment and reducing procurement and operational expenses. The savings help bring down the cost of treatment for patients. A 2017 case study by The Commonwealth Fund documented that Narayana Health had brought the average cost of open-heart surgery below US$2,000 at the time. By rethinking how hospitals operate, Dr Shetty built a business model that demonstrates how greater efficiency can help more families access specialised medical care. Helping waste pickers become entrepreneurs When Lotfar moved to Bengaluru in 2010, he was struggling to make ends meet as a waste picker. A 2022 report by Tata Trusts documented how his life changed after he began working with Hasiru Dala. By then, he owned four trucks and employed around 20 other waste pickers. Founded in 2015 by Shekar Prabhakar, Nalini Shekar and Marwan Abubaker, Hasiru Dala Innovations is a waste management enterprise that helps informal waste workers build more secure livelihoods and run their own businesses. Hasiru Dala Innovations helps waste pickers become entrepreneurs, creating businesses around the people who keep cities clean. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) These entrepreneurs provide waste collection and management services to residential communities, offices and events. They earn through service fees as well as the sale of recyclable materials. By 2022, the enterprise had supported 24 waste-picker entrepreneurs, who had, in turn, created employment opportunities for around 300 other waste pickers. The model brings the people who have long helped keep our cities clean into the business of managing their waste, giving them opportunities to grow as entrepreneurs. From making papads to becoming business owners In 1959, seven women in Mumbai borrowed Rs 80 and began making papads. Their aim was simple: to earn an income of their own. What began as a small venture became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, one of India's most recognisable household brands. Lijjat Papad provides self-employment to around 45,000 women, giving them a shared stake in the enterprise. Photograph: (Femina) According to its official website , the enterprise provides self-employment to around 45,000 women across 83 branches in 16 states. What makes Lijjat particularly interesting is its shared ownership model. Its women members participate in running the enterprise, and the profits and losses of each branch are shared among its members. For thousands of women, a skill they already possessed became a means of earning an income and having a stake in the business they helped build. More than six decades later, the enterprise offers an example of what women can achieve when they have access to economic opportunities and collective ownership. These five enterprises have taken different paths to growth. Yet, each offers a valuable lesson in how businesses can widen access to opportunities, recognise overlooked talent and help people build better lives for themselves. Perhaps, alongside asking how much a business earns, we could also ask a question that deserves just as much attention: Who grows when the business grows? Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Joel Sartore Photo Ark Wildlife Portraits Document 18,567 Species in 25-Year Mission Reading Time: 3 minutes Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits mark two decades of documenting captive species, giving a naked mole rat, a snowy owl, and thousands of others equal time in the spotlight before any could vanish without being seen. Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits began in 2006 at the Lincoln Children’s Zoo near Sartore’s home in Nebraska, with a single photograph of a naked mole rat. Twenty years later, that modest beginning has grown into the largest archive of its kind, totaling 64,436 individual pictures spanning 18,567 species photographed across more than 60 countries. Sartore envisions the project as a 25-year effort to document every species living in human care worldwide. The project’s methodology has remained deliberately consistent over two decades. Joel Sartore’s Photo Ark wildlife portraits are captured against plain black or white backgrounds, stripping away habitat and context so a tiny frog gets the same visual weight and dignity as an elephant or tiger. This approach levels the playing field between charismatic, widely recognized species and overlooked creatures that might otherwise never capture public attention, such as the Palawan stink badger of the Philippines. Sartore does not handle the animals himself during shoots; instead, he relies on zookeepers and animal care staff to safely position each subject. Some aquatic species are photographed through glass enclosures. At the same time, mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects each present their own logistical challenges, from keeping a chimpanzee calm with a caregiver just out of frame to capturing a camera-shy nocturnal porcupine mid-rest. Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits document animals in zoos, aquariums, and wildlife sanctuaries, not creatures photographed in the wild. This focus reflects the project’s core strategy: captive populations often serve as insurance against extinction, and photographing them creates a permanent visual record regardless of what happens to wild populations facing habitat loss, poaching, or climate pressures. The project’s growth trajectory reveals an accelerating pace. Sartore reached 8,000 species roughly a decade into the project, climbed past 11,000 by 2021, surpassed 16,000 by August 2024, and now stands at 18,567, inching toward documenting the full scope of species held in captivity worldwide. Nearly half of all primate species face extinction risk, underscoring the urgency behind photographing vulnerable groups before populations disappear entirely. Portrait of National Geographic photographer and PhotoARK founder Joel Sartore with a frill necked lizard, Chlamydosaurus kingii. Photo by Douglas Gimesy, courtesy of the National Geographic Society . Beyond still photography, Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits have expanded into books including Birds of the Photo Ark and National Geographic Photo Ark Insects, alongside a three-part documentary series titled Rare: Creatures of the Photo Ark. The United States Postal Service further extended the project’s reach by issuing a pane of 20 stamps featuring endangered species drawn directly from Sartore’s portfolio. Public exhibitions have carried the work well beyond magazine pages and museum walls. The Museum of the Shenandoah Valley hosted more than 40 Photo Ark portraits in 2021, and the project’s 20th anniversary brought a dedicated exhibit, Animals of Earth, to the National Geographic Museum of Exploration in Washington, D.C., featuring approximately 17,000 individual wildlife portraits. Among the project’s notable discoveries, Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits have documented entirely new species, including a wild cat native to Bolivia, the first new wild cat species formally described by researchers in over a century, and an undescribed stick insect photographed at the Budapest Zoo. Such discoveries underscore that even as Sartore races to photograph known captive species, new biodiversity continues to emerge from poorly understood corners of the planet. Sartore has been candid about the scale of the task remaining and his own mortality relative to the project’s ambitious scope. He has said a successor will continue the work if he cannot finish, framing the Photo Ark as an effort designed to outlast its founder, with the portraits intended to serve conservation education long after Sartore is gone. The underlying philosophy driving Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits centers on a simple but urgent principle: no species should disappear before it has a chance to be documented, however humble or unfamiliar it may seem to the public. Each portrait serves as a scientific record, a conservation advocacy tool , and an artistic statement, insisting that every living creature, regardless of size or popularity, deserves recognition as a living work of art worth saving. The post Joel Sartore Photo Ark Wildlife Portraits Document 18,567 Species in 25-Year Mission appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: In a pocket park wedged between busy Montreal roads, the sound of ocean waves now washes over a neighborhood that has long carried a quiet grief - the displacement of islanders who left the Magdalen Islands generations ago and never quite left them behind. Researchers and artists collaborated to pipe in field recordings of coastal life, not as decoration, but as a form of cultural memory made audible, transforming a space people once moved through into one they now seek out. "Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource," says McGill professor Catherine Guastavino, whose team helped design the installation - and the results bear that out, with one resident now visiting specifically for "the boost it gives me afterwards." What the project quietly demonstrates is that the antidote to what alienates us in urban life may sometimes be found not in silence, but in the right kind of listening. It turns out that belonging can be transmitted through frequency, and that a community's sense of home need not be lost just because the geography has changed.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saving Bees From Pesticides and Habitat Loss: Three Steps That Work Reading Time: 3 minutes Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss is possible, and everyday choices make a real difference. Find out how gardens, petitions, and protected land help. Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss is possible, and the plan is already clear. Conservation groups say the work comes down to three actions . First, protect the bee habitat that still exists. Second, add new habitat by planting pollinator-friendly plants in gardens and on public lands. Third, end the worst uses of the pesticides that harm bees. Why does this matter so much? Bees move pollen from flower to flower, helping plants produce fruit and seeds. Around the world, bees pollinate 75% of food crops. That is three out of every four crops. Wild plants lean on bees even more, with 90% of flowering species depending on them. Imagine walking past ten kinds of wildflowers. Nine of them would need bees to reproduce. Losing bees would change both our meals and our landscapes. The problem is growing. As society uses more pesticides, bee populations are plummeting. Pesticides are chemicals made to kill pests, but they can also harm bees. Environment America and its state groups, including Environment Georgia, are pushing for change. One campaign asks Amazon to stop selling bee-killing pesticides. Another asks the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to ban the worst uses of these chemicals. A third petition asks the EPA to pause glyphosate, a common weed killer, until it is proven safe. Each petition gives the public a direct way to push for change. Those voices matter for saving bees and their habitat. Large retailers influence which products reach home gardens. Asking them to drop bee-killing pesticides targets the problem at its source. That makes it easier for everyone to save bees from pesticides and habitat loss. Pesticide concerns reach beyond bees. The group also tracks neonicotinoids, a widely used class of insecticides that kill insects. They have also raised concerns about harm to freshwater species. Habitat is the other half of the story. Bees need safe places to find food and shelter. Protecting the land they already use comes first. Habitat loss means fewer flowers to feed on and fewer places to nest. When bees lose food and homes, whole colonies struggle. That is why saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss must go hand in hand. Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss must go hand in hand, since fewer flowers to feed on and fewer places to nest cause whole colonies to struggle, making protection of the land bees already use the first priority. Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Pexels. Recent updates from the group highlight habitat protection for the rusty patched bumblebee. They also point to roadsides as places where pollinators can thrive. These projects show how saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss can happen close to home. Learning is part of the solution too. The group offers a recorded Save the Bees web-bee-nar, which is an online presentation. Another article explains where bumblebees go in winter and how people can help them. Small efforts build on each other. Each new patch of flowers gives bees another place to feed. Each product you buy instead of one from a shelf lowers the risk they face. Research matters as well. The group urges protection of the U.S. Bee Lab, which works to save bees. Science helps people choose the right steps. Speaking up for saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss takes only a few minutes. The group invites people to add their names to its Amazon and EPA campaigns. Public pressure shows companies and agencies that many people care about bees. Anyone with a garden can add habitat. Pollinator-friendly plants give bees food nearby. Public lands can help too. Some states already have policies to protect pollinators, and the group has published a snapshot of those actions. Gardeners can also think twice before buying bee-killing pesticides. A single garden may seem small. Even a window box or a pot on a front step can serve pollinators. Together, these spaces give bees more places to feed across neighborhoods and cities. Each person has a role in saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss. Homeowners can plant flowers and shoppers can ask stores to change what they sell. Anyone can sign a petition and share what they learn with neighbors. See also: Peru Grants Legal Rights for Stingless Bees in Global First Bees support the food on our plates and the wild plants around us. The tools to protect them already exist. Will you plant a garden, speak up, or do both? Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss starts with small choices. It becomes a real change when many people make them. items.descriptionOriginal: "Bhandiwala, bhandiwala." For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas , he collected old clothes , traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused. He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them. But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little. That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi. Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas. "Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly," he says. "We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages." Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence. His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach. According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas , whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation. From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala . He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three. In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste. He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO. The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners? In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use. "Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved," he tells The Better India . The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead. "At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system," he says. People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils. Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai. They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. "I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends," he recalls. "The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution." TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it," he explains. What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them? TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free. A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles. The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner. The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally. The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use. That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place," Vikram says. "We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be." Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners. Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route. TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders. It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation. Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use. Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre. For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations. TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected. 'Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work' TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households. TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work. Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers. "We had to go and search for clothes ourselves," he says. "Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular." For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar. He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat. Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes. "The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect," he says. Now, he receives reusable garments from the team. "Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular," he adds. He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine. Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations. Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping. "Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work," he says. These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold. What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them. Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again? Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model. "The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it," Vikram says. "There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system." Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work. According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline. It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network. 17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next? The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests. Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month. The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them. For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place. There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested , the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply. The team can track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from. For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning. He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens. What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to. All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

items.titleOriginal: “I Heard a Barnacle”: How Paying Attention to Nature’s Background Noise Can Reveal Animal Secrets
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Phil Starks, αναπληρωτή καθηγητή βιολογίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο Tufts, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Κατά τη διάρκεια τεσσάρων ημερών στην Ολυμπιακή Χερσόνησο της Ουάσιγκτον, είδα έναν Ολυμπιακό…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Phil Starks , an associate professor of biology at Tufts University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot , a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook . Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight. Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point , when I heard a barnacle. While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop. As a professor who teaches about animal behavior , I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history . It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise. Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again. At Low Tide My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention. At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone , the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation, and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape. At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle . Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another. The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere. Watch honeybees fly around and see what you notice. When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees , I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures. Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing. A Web of Assumptions Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means. Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example . Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta , a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t. Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments, or stages of life. Muhammad Mahdi Karim/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA This orb-weaver rests on the stabilimentum of its web. I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place. That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does. Seeing Isn’t Knowing The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it. After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.” Aleria Jensen/NOAA/NMFS/AKFSC via Flickr How would you confirm these barnacles made a sound? I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells, and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop. Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows. Look Again For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist , a simple sequence helps: Notice something. Describe it carefully. Ask what else could explain it. Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities. Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers, or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background. Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place. And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before. I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough. RELATED: What Are the Mysterious Creatures Quacking Under the Sea? We’re a Step Closer to Finding Out

items.titleOriginal: Fall hunger is real: four reasons your appetite changes with the season
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Ίσως έχετε προσέξει να επικρατεί τις τελευταίες εβδομάδες. Τελειώνετε το μεσημεριανό γεύμα και μια ώρα αργότερα πηγαίνετε ήδη πίσω προς την κουζίνα. Το μπολ με τη σούπα που θα σε είχε χορτάσει τον Μάιο μόλις και μετά βίας κάνει ένα βαθούλωμα, και κάπου γύρω στις τέσσερις θα ανταλλάξεις σχεδόν τα πάντα με μια ζεστή φέτα κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Maybe you’ve noticed it creeping in over the last few weeks. You finish lunch, and an hour later you’re already drifting back toward the kitchen. The bowl of soup that would have filled you up in May barely makes a dent, and somewhere around four o’clock you’d trade almost anything for a warm slice of something with cinnamon on top. It’s easy to blame the pumpkin bread and cider doughnuts suddenly everywhere you look, and they’re certainly not helping. But if you’ve been feeling hungrier in the fall, there’s more going on than seasonal temptation. Your body is responding to shorter days, colder air, and some very old instincts, all at the same time. Registered dietitian Lyndsay Hall of JM Nutrition walked through what’s behind that bigger appetite, and the good news is that none of it means you’re doing anything wrong. Why you feel hungrier in the fall Old instincts that haven’t caught up For most of human history, the end of summer meant leaner months were coming. “For those living in colder climates, fall signifies the transition from summer to winter, when historically food access would have been limited in the coming months, so people would eat more and put on some extra weight intentionally to help them get through the cold winter season,” Hall said. Your grocery store stays stocked all year, of course, but your body doesn’t know that. Like animals building up reserves before hibernation, some of that seasonal pull toward eating more may be wiring we’ve carried with us for a very long time. Staying warm takes energy Cold weather asks more of you physically, too. “When we start to feel physically cold, our bodies will expend more energy trying to keep us warm (i.e., by shivering) and diverting more blood flow to organs to keep them up and running,” Hall said. More energy spent means your body sends stronger signals to refuel. Less sunlight, shifting moods Then there’s the light, or the lack of it. “Many people experience a drop in serotonin levels during the fall and winter months due to decreased sun exposure and the cold weather making it difficult to get outside as often as we might during the summer months,” Hall said. Lower serotonin can affect hunger and fullness cues, making cravings stronger and meals feel less satisfying. For some people, the darker months bring more than a mild case of the winter blues . If low mood, fatigue, or changes in appetite start to feel heavy or stick around, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor, since seasonal affective disorder is common and very treatable. Holidays on the horizon Fall also kicks off the stretch of the year when so many gatherings revolve around food. “Over time, we have created psychological associations between certain times of year and eating more or indulging. Thanksgiving, for example, occurs in the fall months and is often centered around eating that many look forward to,” Hall said. The same goes for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year’s, when the dishes on the table tend to be rich, hearty and tied up with memories. Staying satisfied through fall and winter None of this calls for a diet or a calorie tracker. Hall’s approach is to lean on three things that help meals stick with you longer: protein, fiber, and healthy fats. “Protein and fiber help to keep us physically satiated for longer periods of time,” she said. Together with fats, they slow digestion, so a cozy meal keeps you going well into the afternoon. Fold protein into the comfort foods you love Hall suggests stirring Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, or a high-protein plant-based alternative, into muffin batter, pancakes, and quick breads. A splash of milk or a dairy-free version in your oatmeal or morning latte works the same way. Eggs, tofu, fish and poultry can round out casseroles and pasta bakes, too. Let vegetables and legumes do the heavy lifting Soups, stews and chilis are perfect for this. Skin-on potatoes, winter squash, eggplant, peppers, leafy greens and green beans add fiber without changing the spirit of a dish, and apples or pomegranate seeds bring a bright, seasonal crunch to salads. “Beans, chickpeas and lentils are great ways to add both protein and lots of fiber to soups, stews, chilis and stuffed vegetables,” Hall said. Give seasonal baking a fiber boost Seasonal treats can pull a little more weight, too. “Oat bran, chia, ground flaxseed, grated zucchini or carrot, and dried fruits can be easy sources of extra fiber for any baked good or hot cereals,” Hall said. So the next time your stomach rumbles an hour after lunch on a gray November afternoon, you can take it as your body doing what it’s long been built to do. Answer it with something warm and filling, save room for the dishes that only come around once a year, and let the season be one you enjoy at the table instead of second-guessing every bite. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Fall hunger is real: four reasons your appetite changes with the season first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance. How the Alzheimer’s pill works A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory ,” she said. That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK , called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function ,” she said. A tablet instead of an infusion The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.” Phase 3 trial results in detail 13 countries, 604 key participants The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD , enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said. The subgroup question The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation. Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment Regulators and further trials None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition. A different route against dementia The stakes are large. Alzheimer’ s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Reading Time: 2 minutes Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Picture a weekend camping trip where your devices stay charged, your food stays fresh, and you have everything you need to enjoy a comfortable escape, all without using more energy than necessary. It might sound like a balancing act, but sustainable outdoor living is becoming easier thanks to smarter technology and a few simple changes in how we use energy. Whether you love camping, traveling in an RV, or entertaining in your backyard, your energy habits can have a bigger environmental impact than you might realize. Fortunately, reducing that impact doesn’t have to mean giving up the little comforts that make spending time outdoors so enjoyable. Make Better Use Of Natural Resources Nature already provides some of the resources you need to enjoy outdoor living comfortably. Making the most of natural daylight, for example, can significantly reduce your reliance on artificial lighting. Try planning outdoor activities around daylight hours and positioning your campsite or seating area to maximize natural light. When evening arrives, solar-powered lanterns and energy-efficient LED lights can provide illumination without consuming large amounts of electricity. Solar technology has also made it easier to generate electricity in remote locations, allowing you to enjoy modern conveniences while reducing your dependence on traditional power sources. Choose Smarter Ways To Power Your Adventures Keeping your essential equipment running is often one of the biggest challenges of spending extended periods outdoors. From charging smartphones to powering portable refrigerators, reliable electricity can make your adventures much more comfortable. However, not every activity requires a large generator or constant access to mains electricity. Portable power stations, rechargeable batteries, and solar-compatible equipment can offer practical alternatives. Looking at the equipment available from Power and Pedal can help you find power solutions suited to different outdoor activities . Choosing equipment that matches your energy requirements can reduce unnecessary consumption while ensuring you have sufficient power when you need it. Think Carefully About Your Outdoor Equipment It’s easy to accumulate gadgets and appliances when you enjoy outdoor activities, but not everything needs to be powered by electricity. For example, a well-insulated cooler might be sufficient for a weekend trip, eliminating the need for an electric refrigerator. Similarly, investing in quality thermal clothing and blankets can help you stay comfortable during cooler evenings without relying heavily on electric heating. When electrical equipment is necessary, prioritize energy-efficient models and maintain them properly to extend their lifespan. Plan Ahead To Avoid Wasting Energy Good preparation is one of the simplest ways to improve your outdoor energy habits. Charging devices before leaving home, downloading entertainment for offline use, and checking equipment before traveling can reduce unnecessary power consumption. Planning meals carefully can also help. Preparing ingredients in advance and choosing dishes that require less cooking time can reduce fuel use, especially on longer camping trips. Make Sustainability Part Of Your Outdoor Lifestyle Creating a more sustainable outdoor lifestyle doesn’t require dramatic changes. Often, it’s the smaller decisions that make the greatest difference when repeated consistently. By making thoughtful equipment choices, using renewable energy where practical, and avoiding unnecessary waste, you can reduce your environmental footprint without compromising your enjoyment. The goal isn’t to eliminate energy use entirely. It’s to use the energy you need more efficiently, allowing you to enjoy comfortable outdoor adventures while taking better care of the natural spaces you love exploring. The post Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? appeared first on Happy Eco News .
