items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Reading Time: 8 minutes 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Health care produced roughly 8.5 percent of all US greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 , according to a 2020 analysis in Health Affairs that put the sector’s total at about 553 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent. My argument here is simple: healthcare SaaS, the software a clinic rents over the internet instead of running on its own machines, is one of the cheapest ways for a practice to shrink its share of that number, and most of the savings show up in the budget too. Now picture one family clinic. Behind the front desk sits a back room lined with manila folders, a shredding bin and a fax machine that still rattles every afternoon. Across the hall, a server closet hums all night with its door propped open because the room runs hot. That clinic is not a villain. It is just carrying what I call everyday carbon : the emissions that come from paper, idle servers, car trips and supplies that expire on a shelf. None of it is dramatic. All of it adds up, and almost all of it can be trimmed without touching a single clinical decision. I have spent years building and fixing software for clinics and hospitals, from appointment tools for two-doctor practices to records systems for regional hospital groups. The five changes below are the ones I have seen stick. 1. Paperless records and e-prescribing empty the archive room Before the switch, a typical small practice runs on paper that moves. Charts travel from the shelf to the exam room and back. Prescriptions get printed, signed, handed over, and sometimes lost in a coat pocket, which means a second trip for the patient. Old files go to an off-site storage unit, and someone drives there whenever a records request comes in. After the switch, the chart lives in a cloud-based electronic health record. A prescription goes straight from the doctor’s screen to the pharmacy, so there is no paper slip and no handwriting for the pharmacist to call about. Intake forms get filled out on a phone the night before instead of on a clipboard in the waiting room. What surprised me the first time I watched a practice go through this was where the real savings hid. The paper itself mattered less than the trips around it: courier runs to the storage unit, patients coming back for a forgotten form, staff driving boxes to a shredding service. One practice I worked with turned its old archive room into a third exam room within a year, which was the moment the owner stopped calling the project “the IT thing.” Nobody misses the fax machine. (Well, one office manager did, for about a week.) 2. A slice of a big data center beats a humming server closet The on-premise server is the quiet energy hog of small health care. It runs around the clock, needs its own cooling, gets replaced every few years, and in most clinics I have visited it sits mostly idle outside office hours. Backups often mean a second machine, or a drive someone takes home on Fridays. Large cloud data centers do the same work far more efficiently, and the numbers on this are striking. A Berkeley Lab analysis published in Science found that from 2010 to 2018, global data center computing output rose 550 percent while energy use rose only 6 percent , with most of the gains coming from big operators running highly efficient facilities. When a clinic moves its records, billing and scheduling to a SaaS product, it trades a single half-used box for a tiny, well-managed slice of one of those buildings. Off-the-shelf products cover most of what a typical clinic needs, but not everything. A fertility center with an unusual lab workflow, or a rural health network that wants its own patient app tied to existing systems, often ends up working with a partner that offers healthcare software development services to build the missing piece. My advice to anyone in that position is to make the green choices at the design stage: pick a cloud region on a cleaner power grid, decide how long logs and imaging files stay in fast storage before they move to cheaper cold storage, and stop the system from keeping five copies of the same scan. Building those rules in from day one costs very little. Retrofitting them into a live system full of patient data means migrations, compliance reviews and weekend downtime, and in my experience that costs far more. One pushback comes up in nearly every conversation I have about this. Skeptics raise a fair objection: the cloud does not cut emissions, it just moves them into giant data centers, and with AI pushing demand up, those buildings are only getting hungrier. Part of that is true. AI is driving a wave of new data center construction, and it deserves close scrutiny. But a clinic is not choosing between the cloud and zero emissions. It is choosing between the cloud and a lone server in a closet with a window air conditioner, and the Berkeley Lab work shows that the efficiency gains landed at the large operators. A clinic can also ask its vendor which region hosts its data and pick one on a cleaner grid, which is a settings change, not a construction project. 3. Telehealth takes car trips off the road without anyone noticing The most visible change is also the easiest to measure. Every follow-up visit that happens over video is a round trip that never happens, and for patients in rural areas that round trip can eat half a day. A national study published in The American Journal of Managed Care in 2025 looked at claims for 44.7 million insured US adults from April to June 2023. Scaled to the whole insured adult population, the researchers estimated that telemedicine averts between 21.4 million and 47.6 million kilograms of CO2 every month , roughly the monthly emissions of 61,000 to 130,000 gasoline cars. The authors call the effect modest relative to all of health care, and they are right to. Still, that is a cut that came almost entirely from visits people preferred anyway. In the practices I have worked with, the clinics that get the most from telehealth are the ones that decide on purpose which visits belong on video. Medication check-ins, test result reviews and most mental health sessions move online well. A sprained ankle does not. There is a second, smaller commute hiding in the same change. Once records, billing and scheduling live in the cloud, the people who handle them no longer have to sit next to the server. I have seen coding and billing teams move to two office days a week, which takes a few more cars off the road and frees up desk space the clinic was paying to heat and cool. The patient keeps the afternoon. The planet keeps the gas. 4. Smarter scheduling and inventory keep vials out of the trash Waste in a clinic is rarely one big mistake. It is a slow trickle of small ones: a box of supplies ordered twice because nobody checked the cabinet, a vaccine lot that expired behind a newer one, a refrigerator that failed on Saturday night and was found on Monday morning. Before SaaS, inventory usually lives in a spreadsheet or a clipboard that one person understands. Orders go out “just in case,” because running short feels worse than overbuying. After the switch, stock levels connect to the appointment calendar, so the system knows that next week has twelve flu shot appointments and only ten doses on hand. It flags lots that are close to expiring so staff use them first, and a cheap temperature sensor in the vaccine fridge sends an alert to a phone the minute something goes wrong. I once watched a pediatric practice lose a full fridge of vaccines to a weekend power fault. After they added a connected sensor, the next fault triggered a text at 2 a.m., a staff member drove in, and the doses moved to a backup unit before any of them warmed up. Nobody wrote a sustainability report about it. It was simply less waste. Scheduling tools help in a quieter way. Automated text reminders cut no-shows, which means fewer wasted slots and fewer rebooked trips. For home health teams, route planning groups nearby visits together, so nurses drive less and see more patients in a day. The software does not care about carbon at all. It cares about minutes and miles, and the carbon follows. 5. Remote monitoring keeps patients home and out of the ambulance The last change reaches past the clinic walls. Patients with heart failure, high blood pressure or diabetes can now send daily readings from a connected scale, blood pressure cuff or glucose meter, and a nurse sees a warning sign days before it becomes an emergency. Evidence from the research side is encouraging, though not unanimous. A 2025 meta-analysis in Cureus pooled 15 studies, nine of them randomized trials, and found that remote patient monitoring reduced heart failure hospitalizations , with the strongest effect from implanted monitors and a smaller one from simpler home devices. The authors rated their confidence in the hospitalization result as moderate, which is an honest grade for a field that is still maturing. Here is where I go a step further. Every avoided hospital stay also means an ambulance ride that did not happen, a bed that did not need heating and cooling for four days, and a stack of single-use supplies that never got opened. The meta-analysis did not count any of that, so this is my own extrapolation. But anyone who has seen how much material a single admission consumes will find it hard to argue the other way. For patients, the benefit is simpler. They sleep in their own beds. What changes when a clinic makes all five moves? Put side by side, the before and after look like this. Practice Before After with SaaS Records and prescriptions Paper charts, printed scripts, fax, off-site storage runs Cloud health record, e-prescriptions sent straight to the pharmacy IT infrastructure Server closet running around the clock with its own cooling Hosted in large data centers, where Berkeley Lab found compute grew 550 percent on 6 percent more energy (2010 to 2018) Routine visits Every follow-up means a car trip Suitable follow-ups on video, an estimated 21.4 to 47.6 million kg of CO2 averted each month across insured US adults (2023 data) Supplies and scheduling Overordering, expired stock, missed fridge failures, no-shows Stock tied to the calendar, expiry alerts, fridge sensors, automated reminders Chronic care Problems surface in the emergency room Daily readings from home, fewer heart failure hospitalizations in pooled studies None of these rows asks a clinic to become a climate organization. Each one is a normal operations upgrade that happens to shrink everyday carbon along the way. Where can a clinic start this quarter? You do not need a sustainability officer to begin. Most everyday carbon sits inside decisions a practice manager already makes, so the steps below fit into budgets and meetings that exist today. Count the paper before you cut it. Spend one week tracking what gets printed, faxed, couriered or driven anywhere. The list is usually shorter than people fear and points to two or three workflows worth moving online first. Start with whatever generates car trips, because those carry the biggest footprint. Ask every software vendor where your data lives. A good SaaS provider can tell you which cloud region hosts your records and whether that region runs on a cleaner grid. If your vendor cannot answer, that tells you something about how closely they watch their own infrastructure. The same question belongs in every new contract. Make video the default for follow-ups that do not need hands. Sit down with your clinicians and agree on a short list of visit types that start as virtual unless the patient prefers otherwise. Patients in rural areas will thank you first. Review the list every six months, since comfort with video tends to grow. Connect the supply room to the calendar. Even a basic inventory module that knows upcoming appointments will stop most double orders. Add a connected temperature sensor to any fridge that holds vaccines or biologics. It is one of the cheapest insurance policies a clinic can buy. Write a retention rule for data, not just for paper. Federal and state law set how long medical records must be kept, so start there, then decide what happens to everything else: old logs, duplicate image files, test exports. Data that nobody needs still sits on powered drives somewhere, and a clear rule keeps your cloud bill and your footprint from creeping upward. A greener clinic in 2030 might look like this What follows is a picture of what is possible, not a forecast. It is a Tuesday morning in 2030. The front desk has no printer. The room that once held folders is an exam room with a window, and the old server closet stores yoga mats for the staff wellness class. Half of today’s follow-ups happen on video, so the parking lot has empty spaces. A home nurse’s route was planned overnight, with four visits on the same side of town. In the vaccine fridge, every vial is in date, because the system flagged the oldest lot last week and the team used it first. Three heart failure patients sent their morning weights before breakfast, and one of them got a phone call and a medication adjustment instead of an ambulance ride. Nothing in that scene requires a breakthrough. Every piece of it exists today. The greenest clinic of 2030 will not look heroic, just quietly well organized. The post 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A wristband developed at the University of Nottingham sends small electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, their tics settle within moments of switching it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. Arielle and Karissa also get into a Greek ship that turned seven years of beach trash into a pollution map, a cancer therapy helping people with Céline Dion’s rare condition walk again, and the real reason you want to cancel plans you were excited to make. Learn more about April Surac and NeuraSensa: https://www.instagram.com/neurasensa/ If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Welcome and catch-up Arielle: Hi, I’m Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome to The Optimist Daily’s Weekly Roundup. How are you doing, Karissa? Karissa: I’m doing well over here. I’m feeling grateful and grounded as we head into the Thanksgiving week next week here in the US. Arielle: Do you have any fun Thanksgiving plans? Karissa: Um, I have multiple Thanksgivings actually I’ll be attending. So this weekend will be my Thanksgiving with my immediate family because everyone is kind of doing different things on actual Thanksgiving Day. And then I’ll be spending actual Thanksgiving with my partner’s family, so multiple celebrations going on this week. Arielle: Aw, that’s cute. And speaking of Thanksgiving, we are actually going to be missing next week’s full episode. We will have just a short greeting from our Optimist Daily family to yours. You can keep an eye out for that, or an ear out for that earlier in the week. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. Well, before we head into anything else, Arielle, how is everything with you? Arielle: Things are good. I was telling you before we hit record that my personal trainer was here today, and it was- excruciating. But yeah, it’s, it’s nice to be working on my strength. I think the benefit of working at The Optimist Daily is that you are exposed to so many solutions just for lifestyle changes that are going to help you live a healthier life and a longer life hopefully. And so yeah, even though the workouts are, uh, brutal sometimes- there’s always light at the end of the tunnel, and I know that it’s for my long-term health, and that kind of motivates me throughout the whole thing. Stay connected and support our work Karissa: There’s just so many great solutions on The Optimist Daily that we get the benefit of learning from. If you want these solutions to your inbox every day, we have a free daily newsletter, and we also have a weekly edition as well. The link to sign up for that is in the show notes. Arielle: We are also on all social media platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. There you can get more bite-sized versions of full solutions. As always, we welcome any comments, questions, or feedback. You can engage with us on those social platforms. You can slide into our DMs, or you can email me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. Karissa: We love to hear from you, and we also love when you share all these solutions in any format, whether you’re forwarding the newsletter, sharing this podcast, and leaving a good review, or reposting to your followers. Arielle: And it’s a wonderful and free way to support our mission. We are so, so grateful for The Optimist Daily community. You guys make this work so special and so meaningful. We appreciate every single like, follow, share, but we also have huge love for our Emissaries, people who financially donate to The Optimist Daily, whether that’s a one-time thing or a regular monthly or annual donation. Emissaries help us continue our mission, pushing it forward. Without them, we wouldn’t be able to do this amazing work. If you wanted to become an Emissary, now is a great time to do that, because we set a goal to get 100 new Emissaries by the end of this year. And I think we’ve maybe surpassed the halfway point at this moment in time? Karissa: We’re just about halfway there, yeah, to our Emissary goal. So help us cross that finish line by the end of the year so we can start off 2027 on an optimistic note, and just get these solutions to as many people as possible. This week’s solutions Arielle: Well, with all of that said, shall I jump into the solutions of the week? Karissa: Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news. “8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning” Arielle: The first solution we have is a lifestyle solution, something that all of us can apply to our lives right now to make it better, and the title is “8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning.” So this is especially for those of us who have a lot of flexibility regarding our schedule, for our remote workers and the like. But do you know when it’s 2:00 PM and you, you can’t really say where the morning went? Two time management experts say the fix for this doesn’t start when your alarm goes off. It actually starts the night before, and it’s way less intense than the really popular two-hour routines that are all over social media that, like, incorporate a bunch of, I don’t know, early morning journaling, and a stretching routine, and an ice plunge, and whatever the latest wellness trends are. Yeah. It can be a lot more simple. I think a lot of us will not be surprised that the number one morning habit, according to Julie Morgenstern, is about your phone. No screens for the first hour after you wake up and the last hour before bed. She compares managing phone time to managing sugar, and I have to say, I am not good at this. Karissa: Yeah. I, I am not good at managing sugar or screen time, so that’s a good comparison. Arielle: Yeah. I, uh… It’s so tempting, especially with the alarm on my phone. I swipe to turn the alarm off, and suddenly I’m already looking at the screen. So I think an analog old-school alarm clock might be a pretty good fix for this. Another habit that she says starts the morning off on the right foot is to begin the workday with the hardest, most important task. So even if the rest of the day falls apart, you’ve done the thing that matters most, that has the most impact. These are all really kind of simple things that you can do or keep in mind when you’re going through your morning. Karissa, what’s the first thing you do when you wake up? Karissa: Well, I mean, I do look at my phone first thing because I’m also swiping to turn off my alarm. So in turn, I’m also looking at all those notifications for a second before I get out of bed, and then I do have my little morning routine. I’ll get up, wash my face, brush my teeth, feed my cat, and put on a pot of coffee, and get some breakfast going. What about you? Arielle: After I have that quick minute on my phone, I also set the kettle to make my tea, and while that’s boiling, I’ll brush my teeth and usually do a little tidy up of the house because this is also my office, so I can’t focus if it’s kind of messy. Luckily, my dog makes me go out. So I do have, like, 20 to 30 minutes of just being out in nature and getting as much sunlight as I can, and I think that counts as one of these microbursts of self-care, which is defined as 5 to 20 minutes of doing something that recharges you. According to this article, the ideal morning routine has three or four elements max. Anything more and you’re setting yourself up for feeling guilty for missing something on a certain morning, or if you have, like, a long checklist of things to do, then it can put a lot of pressure on you as well. Um, so yeah, I did also like that aspect of the article that really emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be complicated. We’re not going through all of the tips here, like what to do the night before, but I highly recommend you check out the article for some more morning routine inspo. Karissa: Yeah, 100%. “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial” Arielle: All right. The next solution is titled “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial.” There’s a wristband out of the University of Nottingham that sends tiny electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, it calms their tics the moment they switch it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. I actually have a cousin who has Tourette’s. And his tics are not so… They’re, they… Like, he can go through the world and navigate it fine, but you can tell that he’s putting a lot of energy towards suppressing a lot as well. Yeah. I can only imagine how life-changing a device like this is that’s kind of subtle and elegant and simple and has a really big impact on just the mental and physical space that suppressing tics has, and also just having to go through the world with people staring at you, not really understanding what’s going on. The source for this article came from the BBC, and I actually took a minute to watch their video on this, and I highly recommend watching the video so that you can kind of get a better sense for how much impact this small device has on people. Karissa: Yeah. And how exactly does it work? Arielle: So how it works is kind of wild. There’s rhythmic pulses to the median nerve cha- which changes activity in the parts of the brain that control movement. In a trial of 121 people, tics dropped by about 25% on average, and it even works for people who don’t have Tourette’s. There was another teenager named Ollie, and he has a functional neurological disorder which makes his neck move constantly without him having any control over it. And when he tried the device, it also just completely stopped the neck movements. There’s a lot of potential for this wearable neurotech to positively affect the lives of people with Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety or even OCD. “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms” Arielle: The next solution is titled “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms.” Okay, so we’ve already talked about the midterms, but we haven’t talked about this specific area of it. I think most people have never eaten foie gras in their lives, and yet it produced some of the most lopsided votes of election night. Animals came out of these midterms surprisingly well, and there’s a pattern in what passed and what didn’t that I found quite interesting. First of all, do you know how foie gras is made? Have you ever eaten it, Karissa? Karissa: Never eaten it, and I didn’t really know much about it until this article actually. Arielle: Yeah. I, I wanna say I have never tried it, but I can’t be for certain. I, I- worked a lot in the hospitality industry and, uh, tried a lot of different things, but it makes me feel a bit bad if I, if I had, because they basically, like, force feed ducks. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Um, or is it geese? But they- I think it’s geese, yeah … force feed them, and it produces this pâté-like, um I’m not describing this well, but people who know foie gras, you know what I’m talking about. Yeah. And those of you who don’t, look it up ’cause it is a l- well, it’s kinda disturbing. Um, so DC voted 73% and Denver 66% to ban foie gras sales, and a DC chef has been hosting foie gras tasting dinners to fund a lawsuit against the ban. So, yeah. Oh. There’s a, a little bit of tension there. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Colorado rejected a constitutional right to hunt and fish, and the fight came down to two words: traditional methods, which critics said could have brought back leg-hold traps and poison as, um, as hunting strategies. Denver voters said no to banning fur and slaughterhouses in 2024, but yes to banning foie gras now. So it seems like narrow bans on one practice seem to have a much easier time going through than ones that take on a whole industry for, of course, concerns about employment and yeah, having to restructure or get rid of a whole industry. Um- so more people are actually paying attention to how their food is produced, even when they’re not really changing their diet. Like, they’re not going vegan, they’re not going vegetarian, but they are concerned about how their food is produced and where it comes from. “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map” Arielle: The next solution is titled “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map.” The team that’s doing the cleanup isn’t just picking up trash. They’re noting down every single piece of it. This project consists of one ship, 20 people, five inflatable boats, and 1,140 tons of trash pulled off remote shores since 2019. For a visual, that’s 22 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of pollution. They’ve built what they say is the largest marine pollution database in the Mediterranean, and university researchers are using it to map plastic on the seabed. The data led them somewhere they didn’t necessarily expect. A lot of the trash came from inland, from rivers and illegal dumps, so they also started a second program on land. Beach cleanups are pretty popular, but there’s growing frustration that cleaning up the beach doesn’t necessarily stop the flow, or it doesn’t nip the issue in the bud. But it’s nice to see that citizen science and cleanup data are increasingly shaping policy on plastics. “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it” Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with you before I hand it over to Karissa is a Local Changemaker. This one’s titled “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it.” This week’s Local Changemaker is April Surac, a Florida teenager who grew up in her family’s furniture workshop and has a younger sister who has autism. Her installations are made of fabric with sensors built in, so the surfaces shift under your hand and the light and sound change as you move through the room. They’re designed for people with autism and people with sensory or cognitive differences, including dementia. More than 15,000 people have experienced the installations, and she sent over 250 sensory kits to families, schools, and hospitals. And she funds a lot of it with her own savings. I think she started this when she was only 16 or 17, which is so impressive. She’s also a 2025 Barron Prize winner, and she’s now working on gallery commissions in New York, LA, and London. Plus, she is developing a wearable sensory tool, and she’s moving towards patents for that. I think it’s really encouraging that a lot of people are growing in their awareness and compassion for diverse bodies and experiences. Sensory-friendly hours are popping up at museums, grocery stores, and movie theaters, which comes from people just realizing how much public spaces assume about our bodies. It’s wonderful to see the shift from accessibility compliance to designing for everyone from the very beginning of a project. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. And I really loved that she had a line that said, “Design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” And that’s something we don’t see enough of in our world. So I think this is just such a fascinating, uh, story, what she’s doing, and I feel so honored to be able to share her story here on The Optimist Daily as one of our local changemakers this year. “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade” Karissa: “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade.” So homelessness in the US dropped more than 6% last year. That’s about 49,000 fewer people without housing, and the biggest one-year drop in over a decade. One of the biggest points here in this article is that veteran homelessness is down nearly 60% since 2010, and advocates say it’s proof that putting people in housing first with no strings attached actually works. On the other hand, the Trump administration credits immigration enforcement and encampment crackdowns to this decline, but advocates say their data shows cities with camping bans did worse than average. It’s important to note, too, that not everyone saw a drop because people who’ve been homeless for a long time increased slightly, and that’s the group that both sides are fighting over the best way to help them. But yeah, I mean, in a time where housing affordability is one of the biggest issues in the country right now, this is encouraging news nonetheless. “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling” Karissa: The next solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling.” So you know when you’re the one who made the plans, and then an hour before you’re supposed to leave, you’re on the couch drafting a text reading, “I’m so sorry, something came up,” or, “I feel sick.” There’s actually a name for this experience, and there’s a surprisingly simple trick for getting out the door anyway. Arielle, have you had this feeling before? Arielle: Oh my gosh, this is so relatable. I do find myself kind of dreading plans, and I try not to cancel. I try to push myself through it, but there are some days where I’m just like, “Ooh, I don’t wanna hop on my bike and go through the rain,” and- you know, I don’t wanna see anyone. I don’t wanna talk to anyone. I’m so tired. So yeah, this solution definitely spoke to me. Karissa: And I’m sure probably all of us have been there at some point or another. But this feeling is called anticipatory anxiety. 55% of Gen Z say they feel relief when plans get canceled, and a UK survey found that 68% of under 34s have flaked. But there’s a simple therapist-approved trick to get over this anxiety. Set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, shower and get dressed without debating it. So kind of just going forward with it without overthinking it. I think flaking has become so normal now that some people kind of dread planning anything, including their own birthdays and events. And in a time where loneliness is being talked about as a public health issue, canceling plans is a small part of this bigger picture. I feel like it’s kind of a lot easier to cancel plans, too, especially ’cause you don’t even have to call someone to cancel. You just send a text. But usually it’s better for all of us to push through and go forward with that connection anyways. Arielle: I like how this article said that part of the strategy is to imagine a moment when you did push through and you did go to whatever event or whatever gathering or, or meetup that you were once dreading. And chances are you ended up enjoying yourself, and you forgot all about that dread that you had before you actually stepped out the door. And there’s a lot of discussion around protecting our own peace, which I think is valid, but it can make it a lot easier to cop out. We have to be really careful about whether or not we are protecting our peace and we do need that break, because sometimes we definitely do need to take a moment for ourselves, or if we’re just letting the anxiety take over. “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers” Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers.” Two of the most toxic forever chemicals have dropped by almost a third in England’s rivers over the last 10 years, and in fish by about half. The UK basically banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and the river data now shows the effect, that 30% and 29% drops. But the catch is the chemicals didn’t actually disappear. The total amount is probably the same, but it’s just been diluted and washed out to sea. So it’s still out there, but there’s not as much, you know, going in. There are about 15,000 types of PFAS, and England has just two facilities that can destroy them for good, so not a lot, uh, out there that can get them out of here. PFAS are in the news constantly. They’re in our drinking water, in non-stick pans, rain jackets, and people are increasingly worried about them in their own homes, with good reason of course, because they don’t go away. And the UK government just announced it will start measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies, so we should have more data on, you know, how exactly forever these chemicals are, and hopefully that will inform more policy in the future. “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again” Karissa: The next solution is “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again.” Stiff person syndrome is a rare condition that Céline Dion lives with, and until now, there’s been no real treatment for it. Doctors at the Mayo Clinic tried a therapy that’s normally used for cancer, and some patients who needed help walking are now miraculously back at work. CAR-T therapy is something that takes your own immune cells, reprograms them in a lab, and puts them back to wipe out the cells causing the disease. Patients in this one got a single treatment, and one patient, Jonathan, went from needing his family’s help with basic tasks to returning to his favorite hobbies like hunting and fishing again, and he says he hasn’t had a single episode since. This condition, like I mentioned at the beginning, was, you know, kind of brought into the spotlight by Céline Dion’s diagnosis in 2022. She was part of a documentary that brought this condition to the fore. So yeah, CAR-T therapies are one of the biggest stories in medicine right now, and researchers are also trying it out on lupus, MS, and other autoimmune diseases. But as of now, these therapies are incredibly expensive, so it raises the questions about who will have access to them. But hopefully with all medical breakthroughs and advancements, it will become more accessible to more people who need it. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them)” Karissa: The last solution I have to share is also a lifestyle-oriented one, and has to do kind of with Thanksgiving and the holidays coming up. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them).” So yeah, this holiday party season is about to start, and this one’s all about the stuff your guests notice but would never mention. This goes over a lot of great, uh, you know, pointers about hosting. One prominent one is the parking and coats problem. A party can be beautifully decorated and still feel chaotic if peoples have to circle the block searching for parking, or if they have to hold their jackets for 30 minutes without somewhere to put them. Arielle: The tip that spoke to me was about letting yourself as a host enjoy the gathering as well, instead of always being concerned with, like, cleaning up or prepping things or grabbing whatever, because the people who are there, the people you invited, are there to presumably spend time with you and each other. And it can put people on edge if you’re just constantly, like, fluttering around and, you know, making sure that everything is running perfectly without actually taking the time to settle in. And that, that is kind of challenging for me. Um, especially because I enjoy cleaning. But that’s definitely something that I’m going to be taking to heart this holiday season. And yeah, there’s a lot of other really great tips here as well. But yeah, exciting to get into the festive spirit. Karissa: That’s all the solutions we had this week on The Optimist Daily. Closing quote Arielle: Before we wrap up this episode, we have an inspiring quote, as usual. Karissa: Yes. The quote is, “My turn shall also come: I sense the spreading of a wing.” And that’s from Osip Mandelstam. Very poetic. Yeah, a poetic end to this edition of the weekly roundup. Thanksgiving sign-off Arielle: Yes. We will be back… Oh, we won’t actually be back next week with a full episode, but we will have a special Thanksgiving greeting from The Optimist Daily team to all of you. But in the meantime, Karissa and I wish you all a very, very happy, restful weekend. items.descriptionOriginal: If you’re sitting down for seafood, should you order the farmed or wild-caught fish? In this day of over-exploited seas, the farmed fillet might seem like a better choice. And yet, in many cases, those farmed salmon or trout also contribute to over-fishing , because they’re raised on diets of wild-caught sardines, herring, anchovies, or mackerel . But researchers have now developed a potential solution to this problem: a meat-free, algal diet that farmed fish can thrive on. As human populations expand, farmed fish are becoming an increasing protein source. Roughly 100 million tons of farmed fish and crustaceans are harvested worldwide each year. In order to feed them, at least 20 millions of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil each year—most of it consumed by farmed predatory species such as salmon and trout. But even non-predatory farmed fish like tilapia have hidden costs, because they’re often raised on cornmeal or soy, requiring agricultural land that might otherwise feed humans directly. A team of researchers at the University of California Santa Cruz has spent years developing fish feeds based on two types of marine algae, called Nannochloropsis and Schizochytrium , which are also being used or studied as sources for biofuels, farm animal feed , and nutritional additives for human foods. In 2020, the team showed that farmed tilapia grew normally on blends of these two algae . In the new study, published October 16 in Antioxidants , they tried feeding these algal blends to a commonly farmed carnivorous fish, rainbow trout. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby both;} Recommended Reading: Solar above, fish below: Double-decker farms could rival US power use After 84 days of aquaculture, trout fed on a 100 percent algal diet showed growth that was similar to trout on a standard fishmeal and fish oil diet. Fish on the algal diet also had similar levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids, including omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (which are considered important for preventing chronic disease in humans). Overall protein levels were also similar in the algal-fed and standard-fed trout, as were levels of essential amino acids and mineral nutrients such as iron, calcium, magnesium, and zinc. Economic analyses suggested that purchase costs for the 100 percent algal feed might be slightly lower than the costs of standard fish-based feeds. The algal feeds and standard feeds were equally efficient at producing fish biomass in both absolute (kg of feed per kg of fish produced) and economic terms ($USD of feed per kg of fish produced). This new research doesn’t solve all of the problems of aquaculture, which also include greenhouse emissions , as well as nitrogen and phosphorus pollution that can spawn hypoxic dead zones in nearby waters. But it’s a step forward. After all, it’s increasingly clear that high-plant, low-meat diets are healthier for both humans and the planet. So shouldn’t our seafood follow the same advice? items.titleOriginal: Cafe Server Returns Bag of $20,000 Left Behind by Couple
items.description: Στο αποκορύφωμα ενός σαββατιάτικου δείπνου στη Σιγκαπούρη, ένας σερβιτόρος καφέ ονόματι Lau Guat Toh εντόπισε μια τσάντα χωρίς επίβλεψη και έκανε ό,τι της ήρθε φυσικά - την προστάτεψε, την έβαλε κάτω από μια κάμερα ασφαλείας και περίμενε. Μέσα ήταν 20.000 δολάρια σε μετρητά, αρκετά για να κροταλίσουν τους περισσότερους, αλλά η Λάου και οι συνάδελφοί της «δεν τόλμησαν να το αγγίξουν», μια λεπτομέρεια που λέει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At the height of a Saturday dinner rush in Singapore, a coffee shop server named Lau Guat Toh spotted an unattended bag and did what came naturally to her - she protected it, placed it under a security camera, and waited. Inside was $20,000 in cash, enough to rattle most people, but Lau and her colleagues "did not dare touch" it, a detail that says more about their character than any declaration of honesty could. The bag's owner, a noodle manufacturer who had rushed off to a friend's wake, returned at 11pm simply trying his luck, and found everything intact. What lingers in the story is the quiet ecosystem of goodness surrounding the moment: a boss who had spent his evening delivering donated soup to elderly residents, a customer whose first response to losing a fortune was not panic but acceptance, and a server who plans to keep her $200 reward as a souvenir rather than spend it. "If something is meant to come, it will come," said the man who lost the money - and somehow, in this small coffee shop in Bedok, it did.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage.
